Mind is empty, dharmas are empty; do not give rise to a second thought. Sitting and cutting off the master, this is truly peaceful.

"Delightful indeed are our brothers. Ascending the hall: advancing, there is nothing before; retreating, there is nothing behind. A hair’s breadth of discrepancy, and one immediately falls into a trap.
On the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month, Dongshan departed from Chadu. Yunmen said, "I would give you thirty blows," yet how could it be otherwise? It is groundless.
Without cause. Receiving birth after receiving birth.

This is the Universal Discourse of Yangshan. Master Tiānyī Huái cited it, saying: An ancient said, "Upon the mountain of the five aggregates is a single expanse of emptiness;
though we pass through its gates together, we do not meet. For immeasurable kalpas we have lived in rented rooms, yet until the end we do not know the owner."
Regarding the "Old Man": Later, an ancient master took up this case and said, "Since he did not recognize him, whom did he ask when he first went to rent?
Tianyi further said, "When the ancients handled it in this way, they were still far from the mark.
Why? You must know that on the road of the dead, there is a place where the living emerge; yet on the road of the living, the dead are countless. Which of these is the road of the living?"
Countless are those who are dead. Which among them is the path of the dead? Where does the living person emerge?
If you can understand this, you will cast off the cap of dripping fat and strip away the stinking cloth robe.
Miaoxi said: "Tianyi was an ancient Buddha; it is beautiful, yet not yet perfect. This crew of incompetent fellows knows only how to step forward, but..."
He realized that the four-sided ground had collapsed. Yangshan could not help but pick him up from the very beginning: "A segment of emptiness atop the mountain of the five aggregates;
the eyes within the skull. Entering and exiting the same gate, they do not meet; where would you even attempt to evade them?"
For immeasurable kalpas you have lived in rented quarters, yet you treat your own ancestral inheritance as if it were the deed of another.
To the very end, you do not recognize your own master; what is the use of such recognition? Since you do not recognize him, whom did you ask when you first began renting?
Seeking further for a guarantor, the ancients handled it in this way—how far removed that is! One might think there is no one to provide witness; why is this?
You must know that on the road of the dead, there is a place where the living emerge; "pointing" does not reach it. On the road of the living, there are countless dead;
"reaching" does not point to it. Which, then, is the place on the road of the dead where the living emerge?
"Where? How? How? Which is the path of the living? There are countless dead people. Lower your voice, lower your voice!
If you can understand this, cast off the cap of dripping fat and strip away the foul-smelling cloth robe; yet even so, you have added one more layer.
Old Man Miaoxi said, 'Tianyi is an ancient Buddha. This is beautiful, but it is not yet perfect. He is accustomed to..."
Black beans were exchanged for human eyes. Although Miaoxi did not know he had already been replaced by Tianyi, do you all know where this falls?
If you do not yet know, you must find a single thread of a path before the black beans have even sprouted;
only then can you penetrate it. What is the message before the black beans have sprouted? Liang.
Jiuyun said: "If you can grasp it here, you will see that very void atop the mountain of the five aggregates. Truly, 'Passing in and out the same gate, we do not meet;
for immeasurable kalpas we have lived in rented houses. Now, let us rejoice at having arrived home, yet in the end we do not recognize the master of the house.
This talk has fallen away. But tell me: was it the ancient masters whose talk fell away, or was it Tianyi whose talk fell away?
The story of Miaoxi falls; the story of Yangshan falls. If you can discern them clearly, consider this:

Yunmen asked a monk, "Is it not the words of the scholar Zhang Zhuo that 'radiant, silent illumination pervades the sands of the Ganges'? When the monk said, "It is," Yunmen let him go—this old fellow has been pardoned.
On the road to Mount Tai, there was a woman who, seeing a monk, asked him the way to Mount Tai. Toward what...?
"Where have you gone? The nun said, "I went straight ahead. As soon as the monk had walked a few steps, the nun said, "What a fine monk you are!
Yet you go off like this again. Later, this story was transmitted to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou said, "Wait until I go there and expose her for what she is.
When Zhaozhou arrived at that place, he asked her the same question, and she gave him the same answer. Upon returning, he said, "The old woman on the road to Mount Tai—I have exposed her for you."
It has been thoroughly scrutinized. Now tell me: how far apart are Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman and Yunmen’s "slipping of the word"?
If you can recognize Zhaozhou’s heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys here, then the three hundred and sixty joints of Yunmen will be pierced through by you all at once.
Xuefeng was serving as the head cook for Deshan; one day, when the meal was late, he himself...
Deshan went down from the hall to beg for alms. Xuefeng asked him, "The bell has not yet rung and the drum has not yet sounded;
where are you going with your alms bowl? Deshan lowered his head and returned to his quarters. "Still water does not harbor dragons," said Yantou upon hearing of this. "That old fellow! he exclaimed.
The final word has not yet been encountered; swords and spears fill the earth. Deshan called out to Yantou, asking, "Do you not approve of me, old monk?
Yantou turned his face around; it was like silk wrapping a stone, as soft as a lump of mud.
The next day, Deshan ascended the hall and indeed acted differently. Yantou clapped his hands and said, "I am glad the old fellow has finally understood."
The final word. Although he only had three years [to live], tell me: was he able to pass through Deshan’s test and emerge, or did he have to bow his head and return to the abbot’s quarters?
Students of the Way must possess an eye that can discern errors from three thousand miles away;
only when you know the point of landing before it has even been pointed out will you succeed. If you wish to seek his final word here, you must examine it until you have seen through it.
Old Lady, your talk has already fallen into error. You must wait until Bodhidharma faces the wall for nine years before you may attain it; otherwise, you must wait for Maitreya’s descent.
Generally speaking, one must polish and refine oneself until clarity is reached, and discern the right and wrong of the past and present.
To understand yourself but not the past and present is for your practice to have not yet reached its goal and your ground to be unsteady.
To understand the past and present but not yourself is for your critical juncture to remain unpenetrated and your vision to be unclear.

You should know that the self is precisely the past and present, and the past and present are precisely the self. Because the ancients did not understand their own selves, they [acted] for your sake...
Within your own domain, if you casually bring forth even a single spark and place it before you, it truly covers heaven and earth and illuminates past and present.
How could there ever be so much as a single thread of emotional consciousness or intellectual views that allows you to engage in speculative interpretation?
As soon as you give rise to a single thought here, wishing to clarify the ancient and modern or to understand this "self," [you have already missed it].
Because of that single character "bright" (ming) and the character "to understand" (hui), it has been divided into two segments. Therefore it is said: "When emotion arises, wisdom is separated;
when conceptualization changes, the essence becomes distinct. But when emotion has not yet arisen, what is there to separate?
You must, right here, smash it into a hundred pieces at once; only then will you no longer perceive the existence of past or present, or of a self. Do not remain merely drifting and indolent.
Wasted time in vain. Until the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, when the eyes fall to the ground, one will not know where one has gone.
Consider, for instance, the two elders, Chief Xian and Elder Biao, who died and were cremated the other day; where are they now?
If you do not know their destination, you will crash into the wombs of donkeys or horses and remain among the various species of beings—altogether...
You have seen it. You people here right now, with both feet planted firmly on the ground—do you know where you are going?
If you can know this, then you will see that before the face of a dead man there is a place for a living man to emerge; and before the face of a living man...
There are countless dead people. The ancient and the modern are oneself; oneself is the ancient and the modern.

Yet this does not hinder the ancient and the modern from being the ancient and the modern, nor oneself from being oneself, nor the dead person from being the dead person, nor the living man from being the living man.
Only then, returning to this very point, one strikes a single round: within a speck of dust or a pore, the oceans of lands and self and other are not separated by even a hair’s breadth.
Duan. Throughout the ten ages of past and present, beginning and end do not depart from the present moment of thought. It is further said: "When lifted up, it exists; when set down, it is gone.
To hold such a view is to perceive intimacy and distance. It is like casting a mirror to produce an image: once the image has formed, where does the light reside?
It is entirely ungraspable throughout the body; it has never been hidden anywhere in the world.

The decline of the Buddha-Dharma has never been more severe than it is now. It relies entirely upon you, the younger and later generations, to give rise to great courage and harbor great aspirations, supporting it with bare hands and bearing its burden on single shoulders. Brothers, how much is at stake! The Dharma-gate is vast and profound.
Do not fail the Buddhas and Patriarchs who established this path and bestowed the compassionate grace of the Dharma-milk.

Do not fail the kings and rulers who provide external protection and the grace of sustaining the land and its people. Do not fail your parents and teachers who nurtured you and granted you the precepts of tonsure.
Do not fail your own resolve to leave the household life and travel as a mendicant. Do not wastefully consume the offerings of the faithful; do not wastefully pass your time.
Time does not wait for man; in the blink of an eye, it is already the next life. If this body is not delivered in this present life, in what other life shall one deliver it?

Do not wait until you are parched with thirst before digging a well; do not wait until the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, when the light of your eyes is about to fall and yet has not fallen, and you are terrified of death while craving life, your hands and feet flailing in frantic confusion like a crab falling into boiling water. Upon reaching that point—
At that time, even if you were to turn back the light of your desires to practice this Way in order to break through birth and death, it would be too late;

you would have failed to apply yourself with sufficient effort. Do not let yourself be blown by a gust of karmic wind into the eighteen layers of the Avīci Hell, where the old man Yama will settle your accounts with a ledger of fire and demand payment for your meals. Will you have any?

An iron collar shall bind your neck; an iron mace shall strike your bones and hips. At that time, you will call out for your father but receive no answer, and you will cry for your mother but hear no sound.
Even if you have a biological father and mother, or biological brothers and sisters, they will be unable to save you.

All the wholesome and unwholesome karma you have committed throughout your life will manifest all at once. You will be pounded by pestles and ground in mills with no end in sight, even if you were to escape.

Excluding those born by transformation, they merely cycle through the six realms of existence, even becoming as small as gadflies, mosquitoes, termites, or ants, bobbing their heads up and down within cesspools.
Truly, it is said that beneath the *kāṣāya*, one loses the human body; this is indeed suffering.
Why not take advantage of the present—while your body is strong and robust, your five limbs are healthy and at ease, and your four members are light and agile—and strike through to the very bottom?

Seek instruction until you understand it clearly. How fortunate that you have again found yourself here in this great mountain and vast marsh, this world of divine dragons, this Dharma cave of the Patriarchs.
The quarters in the Sangha hall are peaceful and bright; the rice gruel and meals are pure and clean; the facilities for hot water and fire are secure and convenient.
If you do not strike through to the very bottom right here, it is your own self-abandonment and self-rejection; you would be content to sink like a stone, remaining base and inferior.
You foolish fellow! If you are truly so ignorant, why do you not consult those who have already awakened?

Whenever you encounter the five periods of formal inquiry and see that man upon the curved wooden seat speaking in such wild and confused ways, why do you not take this to heart and reflect upon it repeatedly within yourself?
What, after all, is the principle behind this? As for the Buddhas of the three periods of time...
It is said that he appeared in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition.

It is said that he opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, awakens one to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and leads one into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This Buddha-knowledge and vision is nothing other than this:
within the twelve periods of the day, every single instance of your bowing, turning, looking down, or looking up, as well as your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

It is simply you, right here and now, shoulder to shoulder and foot to foot, listening to that fellow on the curved bench who beats two pieces of skin and speaks with such clamor and chatter—that which is this single, solitary, bright, and vivid presence.
It is only because you lack self-confidence and cannot directly accept it that you fail to receive this ready-made enjoyment. Mazu called it "this very mind."
This is the Buddha; the Buddha is precisely the mind. Outside the mind there is no Buddha; outside the Buddha there is no mind. "Buddha" has the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*).
This refers to the fact that from immeasurable kalpas past, you have wandered through birth and death, turning your back on awakening and uniting with the dust of sensory objects.
You have been adrift in the cycle of birth and death, submerged in the river of craving, and enveloped by ignorance, afflictions, dullness, and distraction. You require this one crucial point.

If liberation were to manifest before you, you would ultimately be unable to attain it; this is why past sages labored to appear one after another, establishing schools and branching lineages to stimulate the turbid and exalt the pure, the lingering influence of which remains even to this day. Brothers, regarding these two words, "Buddha-dharma":
This is difficult to encounter and difficult to meet. Do not allow yourself to turn over and fall into the realms of other species;
once you have done so, you will no longer hear the Buddha-dharma. You must arouse great courage and advance straight ahead.

Raising the precious Vajra-sword, you must sit upon the heads of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and lie upon their heads, only then will it be achieved. When I, this mountain monk, arrived here, I was honored by the host.
The current assembly is such that they cannot even be lifted by a spoon; their practice and understanding are overgrown and neglected, far removed from the ancients.
It relies entirely upon you, the younger and later generations, to rouse a single breath of indignation and come forth to vindicate the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
The other day, two brothers came to the attendant’s quarters saying they wished to visit the Abbot’s quarters for instruction. I told the attendant that whenever the fifth [day] arrives...
"Attend! I must speak of the section on 'applying effort' (gongfu). Why would he not have understood? And why would he need to come to the abbot’s quarters to hear it? It was right then and there.
Here, there is no Dharma transmitted by mouth or bestowed from heart to heart. Wait for the five future sessions of inquiry."
Let me speak for myself once more on his behalf. I left home at the age of five and served under my superior;
while listening to him converse with guests, I immediately understood that such a matter existed, and I came to believe in it, whereupon I began to practice seated meditation.
From birth, he was dull-witted; he exhausted himself through myriad hardships. At sixteen, he became a monk; at eighteen, he set out on pilgrimage.
With a resolute will, he sought to investigate and clarify this matter. While under the guidance of Master Yuan of Shuanglin Tiejue, he struck out in all directions.
From morning until night, he remained only within the meditation hall, never stepping outside the courtyard. Even when entering the communal quarters, he went no further than...
Later, as he walked with his hands folded across his chest, moving slowly back and forth without glancing left or right, his gaze never extended more than three feet before him.
When the venerable masters of Dongshan wished to teach people to investigate the koan "Does a dog have Buddha-nature?

they would simply, at the very moment miscellaneous perceptions and discursive thoughts arise, lightly raise the single word "Mu" (無) upon the tip of their own noses; as soon as one perceives that the thoughts have ceased, [the truth is revealed].
Furthermore, set it all down at once; simply sit in silence like this. Wait for it to become mature; after a long time, you will naturally realize it yourself.
The approach of the Dongshan school requires such dense and meticulous effort that it is exhausting; often it takes ten or twenty years before one can grasp it.
This is why its lineage has been difficult to sustain. At that time, when a thought suddenly arose within me, I struck it with a blow.
I turned my gaze inward. At the point of this inward turning, this single thought-moment was instantly frozen clear; it was truly limpid and profound, unmoving and unshakable.
Sitting for an entire day passed like the snap of a finger, and I did not hear the sound of the bells or drums at all.
When the midday meal ended and the session concluded, I remained unaware of it. The Elder, hearing that I had sat well, came down from the Sangha Hall.
Look! I once praised him while upon the Dharma seat. In my nineteenth year, I went to Lingyin Temple to register as a guest.
There I met Shan Miaofeng; after Miaofeng passed away, Shiti succeeded him on the abbacy. Ying Dong-sou was in the Guest Office, and I was in the Guest Prefect’s quarters.
I saw the Secretary from Chuzhou say, "Brother Qin, this practice of yours is like stagnant water—it will not suffice for the task. Whether in motion or stillness..."
These two aspects remain divided into two separate parts. I was truly struck by his words;
as soon as I am in my seat, this state manifests before me, yet as soon as I step down from the seat to walk or to pick up the spoon and set down the chopsticks, it vanishes entirely.
He further said that in Zen practice one must give rise to the "doubting mind": great doubt leads to great awakening, and small doubt leads to small awakening.
Awakening. There is no awakening without doubt; one must first doubt the koan before it can be realized.
Although he did not apply himself to formal practice extensively, he had naturally inherited the lineage from Nanquan. Nanquan was the disciple of Songyuan; his words were always upright and correct.
At that moment, I changed my meditation topic and took up "a dried-up shit-stick. I doubted it single-mindedly, here and there, looking at it from every angle.
Looking straight ahead, he changed this *huatou*. His previous way of life was completely thrown into disorder.
Although he had sealed his bedding and did not let his side touch the mat, from morning until evening—whether walking or sitting—he was nothing but dullness and distraction, muddled and agitated.
He could not achieve even a single moment of purity. Having heard of Master Tianmu, he attended him for a long time.
Songyuan. [The master] was Songyuan’s disciple; he had certainly obtained Songyuan’s instructions.

He moved his quarters to settle at Jingci Monastery, where he went to the abbot’s quarters with incense in hand to seek further instruction. After performing nine prostrations, the abbot asked him, "How do you practice?
Thereupon, [the master] explained everything from the beginning in full detail. The abbot said, "Have you not seen how Linji questioned Huangbo three times?"

The great purport of the Buddha-dharma: three times I received severe blows from the staff, and finally, beneath Dayu’s ribs, he struck me with his fist three times and said, "Originally, Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not much; you should simply look at it in this way.
He also said, "When Huixuan resided on this mountain, I went there for a brief visit and entered his room. He raised a koan and said, 'A ready-made case—before you have even entered the gate.'"
"Come here. I am going to give you thirty blows! Just look like this! Thus spoke Master Tianmu.
These words of his were indeed an upward-pointing instruction. My own ailment, however, lies in the state of dullness and distraction;
his medicine did not suit me, so I was not pleased. In my heart, I could not help but say that you do not know how to practice, being merely clever...
Lizhan. In our ordinary practice of seeking instruction, at the conclusion there is one incense stick and three prostrations, which is called "thanking for the causal conditions.
This one incense stick of mine has not yet been burned; as before, I rely on myself.

During my regular sitting meditation, there were seven brothers from the two prefectures of Zhang and Quan who entered into a pact with me to practice seated meditation for two years at Jingci Monastery.
He did not spread out his bedding, nor did his side ever touch the mat. Outside [this group] was the Venerable Xiu, also a native of Zhangzhou, who was not included among these;
he simply walked alone and sat alone. Every day upon his meditation cushion, he was like an iron spike.
When walking on the ground, he held his spine straight, let his two arms hang down, and kept his two eyes wide open.
It was like an iron stake. Morning after morning it was thus; day after day it remained the same.
Every day I went to approach him and speak with him for a moment, but as soon as I saw me coming from the east, he would go off to the west;
as soon as I saw me coming from the west, he would go off to the east. In this manner, for two years, I sought to draw near to him.
A mere trifle; it can no longer be attained. For two years, because I did not reach the end, I was worn out and exhausted.
By day it was like night, and by night it was like day; when walking it was like sitting, and when sitting it was like walking.
It was nothing but a single state of dullness and distraction, rolled into one mass, like a piece of rotting...
It is like trying to find mud that resembles [the original]; one cannot obtain even a moment’s purity. One day, he suddenly reflected:
"I have set out to cultivate the Way, yet it has not entered my grasp; the clothes upon my body are tattered and worn, and my skin and flesh are withered and decayed."
Unaware of it, tears flowed; suddenly, thoughts of home arose. He requested leave to return to his native place, thinking, "From now on, this one letting go—let me let go of everything.
Two months later, he returned to attend the retreat, once again setting everything right from the beginning.

Yet, upon reaching this stage of letting go, his spirit was ten times more vigorous than before. Truly, if you wish to investigate and clarify this matter, you cannot afford not to sleep; you must simply do so.
At midnight, I fell into a deep sleep; only after waking did I regain my spirits.
One day, as I was walking back and forth in the corridors, I suddenly ran into Brother Xiu. Looking at him from afar, I felt only that he was serene and joyful.
He had the air of one who had attained something for himself. As I drew near, he began to speak with me; from this I knew he possessed some realization.
I asked him, "Last year I intended to give you [instruction], yet you merely avoided me whenever we spoke. Why was that?
He replied, "Venerable brother, you are truly a man of the Way who has no leisure even for the task of clipping his nails. He then gave it to me.
He then asked me, "How do you practice? I recounted it to him from beginning to end.
At the conclusion, I said, "Nowadays, I am simply plagued by dullness and distraction; I cannot settle them. He replied, "What difficulty is there?
It is simply that you lack intensity. You must sit firmly upon your meditation cushion, straighten your spine, and..."

His joints support one another; taking all three hundred and sixty bones and eighty-four thousand pores together as a single "Mu" (無), he raises it up in this manner. What further drowsiness or distraction could there be?
I followed his instructions, sought out a thick meditation cushion, placed it upon my seat, and straightened my spine, making each of its joints...
The joints interlock; penetrating to the very top and through to the bottom, throughout all three hundred and sixty bones and joints, one raises [the mind] with a single lift.

It is just like a single person facing ten thousand enemies. The more one exerts force in this lifting, the more one sees. Furthermore, when reaching this point of dispersal, one lifts with all one's life-force.
Suddenly, body and mind are both forgotten; one only perceives before oneself what is like a vast silver mountain and an iron wall.
It was as if so. My walking was thus, and my sitting was thus. For three days and nights, I remained pure and my two eyes did not blink.
On the afternoon of the third day, while standing beneath the three gates, I was walking as if sitting when I suddenly ran into my elder brother, Xiu.
He asked me, "What are you doing here? I replied to him, "I am practicing the Way. He said, "You..."
"What do you call 'the Way'? he asked. I was unable to respond and became increasingly bewildered and distressed.

I intended to return to the hall to practice seated meditation, but after reaching the rear gate, I unconsciously entered the quarters of the Rear Hall. The Head Seat (Shouzuo) asked me, "Brother Qin, how is your cultivation of the Way?
I told him, "It was not right of me to ask so many people; it has utterly prevented me from practicing. He...
He further said, "Just open your eyes wide and look! What kind of principle is this?
When I was presented with this single phrase, he immediately withdrew his body and insisted on returning to sit in the hall. Only then did I turn my body over onto the meditation cushion;
before me, everything suddenly opened up as if the earth had collapsed. At that moment, it could not be presented to others, nor could it be described to others.
It is attained. It is not something of the mundane world that can be illustrated by analogies. At that time, I was free from attachment and in a state of joy;
I descended to the ground to seek out my elder brother. He was at his desk with the scriptures. As soon as he saw me coming, he joined his palms and said, "How joyful! How joyful!
I then took his hand and walked together to the willow embankment in front of the gate, where we paced back and forth.

Within heaven and earth, the myriad phenomena of the forested and the vast—all that has been seen with the eyes and heard with the ears, and all those things previously loathed and discarded—along with ignorance, afflictions, dullness, and distraction, have from the very beginning flowed forth from within the wondrously luminous true nature.
Since then, for more than half a month, they have been manifest before one’s eyes: starkly bare, profoundly still, and vividly pressing upon the senses. They move.

Characteristics do not arise—how regrettable! Had you not met a venerable elder of great vision and great skillful means to settle this for you, it would have been improper to remain seated here, sitting fixedly;
this is called "not being liberated from the ground of views," which obstructs right knowledge and insight.
Every time you fall asleep at midnight, in that state where there is no dreaming, no thinking, no hearing, and no seeing, you again split it into two separate parts.
The ancients spoke of "waking and sleeping being as one," yet you still fail to penetrate this. If the eye does not sleep...
All dreams vanish of their own accord. If the mind does not differ [from its object], then the teaching that "the myriad dharmas are one suchness" has been entirely misunderstood.
Regarding the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients: those with a logical path that can be chewed over may be understood;
however, those without a logical path—like silver mountains and iron walls—cannot be comprehended at all. Even though one is within the assembly of the late Master Wuzu, [if this is so,]...
For many years, whenever he opened his room for instruction, I would take up the "Principal Host" (zhugongzhu) koan and give a leap.

I was careful not to let him raise the "nose of the patch-robed monk" (naseng babei) or the "fangers and claws of the Buddhas and Patriarchs" (fuzu zhuyaya), lest there be no place left for you to open your mouth.
At other times, while he sat upon the Dharma seat, he spoke here and there, yet there was not a single word that struck at the matter within my heart. Furthermore—
I searched through the Buddhist scriptures and ancient sayings from beginning to end, yet not a single word could resolve this illness of mine.

This obstruction in my chest has persisted for only ten years. Later, while staying at Tianyu and Liangshan in eastern Zhejiang with Zhong Shiliang, one day as I was walking before the Buddha hall, I was idly reflecting on things from east to west when suddenly—
However, as he raised his eyes, he touched a single ancient cypress tree;

at that moment, the entire realm of experience he had previously attained was cast away all at once, and the obstructing mass within his breast suddenly dispersed, like emerging from a dark room into the light of day.
It is like making one full circuit; from this point on, there is no longer doubt regarding birth, no doubt regarding death, no doubt regarding the Buddha, and no doubt regarding the Patriarchs.
Only then does one begin to see where the Old Man of Jingshan stands. He deserves exactly thirty blows of the staff. Why?
Because for a person of great power and great capacity, how could there be so many detours? It was like Deshan seeing Longtan.
At the place where the paper candle was blown out, he said: "To exhaust all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the great void;
to exhaust all the world's pivotal mechanisms is like casting a single drop into a vast abyss.

From this point on, I shall wield a white staff that overturns heaven and earth—where would you have a place to approach it? When Master Shaolao was kicked by Mazu, he immediately said: "A hundred..."
The thousand dharma-gates and immeasurable subtle meanings all converge upon the tip of a single hair; here one must recognize the source.
When Gao-tíng saw Dēshān beckon, he immediately strode across. When Yǒng-jia met Cáo-xī, he attained awakening in a single night.
You younger practitioners of later generations, if you wish to inquire into and practice this matter, you must possess this very standard.
"Attain it! Only by possessing this kind of spirit can one succeed. If it were something I had spoken myself, you would not be able to remember even a single character;

to commit it to memory would only mislead you for the rest of your life. Therefore, the great masters of old mostly did not speak of their practical methods, their gates of enlightenment, or their levels of realization, saying that to bind people with substantial dharmas is like 'dust' that cannot be cleansed. This is so.

This is certainly so. There are those who possess great power and have seeds from past lives; they do not come from the place of practice, and there are no tracks or paths by which they can be described.
There are also those who have never applied any effort at all, and thus cannot be described. Then there are those who are half-ripe and half-unripe.
Those who open their mouths yet lack self-confidence truly resemble those who confuse the characters "刁" (diāo) and "刀" (dāo), or "魚" (yú) and "魯" (lǔ).
If one discusses the matter of actual practice, it is like a person walking along a road: having walked one or two *li*, three or four *li*, they then rest;
they can only speak of having walked one or two *li*, three or four *li*. To have walked a hundred or a thousand *li*—

Ten thousand *li*—you have seen the realm of ten thousand *li*, you can speak the words of ten thousand *li*, yet you must know that this matter lies even further, beyond hundreds of thousands of millions of *li*, outside the entirety of the universe. Where is it? Where is it?
You all, hearing such a statement, must personally possess the eye of discernment; each of you must be able to distinguish black from white and right from wrong. Choose!

Only then can blue and yellow be attained. If it were like a duck hearing thunder, or like water poured upon stone, then you would have passed through the bellies of both Master Bodhidharma and the Old Śākyamuni; yet I say that even this is merely idle talk. Long standing.
At Daochang Mountain, during the General Discourse for the Ordination of Monks, a Zen practitioner stepped forward and asked: "The autumn sky is high and the jade dew falls;
yellow chrysanthemums bloom before the eastern fence. When Linji and Deshan deployed the staff and the shout, if they did not seek out those who understand, whom else would they have questioned?"
The Master replied, “One who knows the sound knows it; after that, who else would know?

The monk pressed on, “In that case, water flows cold from the side of the rocks, and wind comes fragrant from within the flowers. The Master replied, “Idle talk. The monk asked, “What is the staff of Deshan?
The Master replied, “It pierces right through your skull. The monk asked, “What is the shout of Linji? The Master replied, “Do you still hear it?”
Mò asked, "I recall that in the past, when Master Linji addressed the assembly, he said:
'Sometimes my single shout is like the Vajra King’s precious sword; sometimes my single shout is like a crouching lion; sometimes my single shout serves as a probe or a decoy;
and sometimes my single shout does not function as a shout. What is the meaning of this? He replied, "From the beginning..."
The questioner asked about the "future. He pressed further, saying, "What is one shout like a vajra-king’s precious sword?
The Master replied, "One must strictly avoid wounding the blade or injuring one's hand. He pressed further, saying, "What is one shout like a crouching lion? The Master replied, "Truly, how pitiable!
He pressed further, saying, "What is one shout acting as a probing rod or a shadow-grass? The Master replied, "It cannot be met face-to-face."

[The student] approaches from behind. [The Master] asks: "How is it that a single shout does not function as a single shout? [The student] replies: "One must investigate it further before one can attain it.
[The student] advances and says: "The probing pole and the shadow-grass are used to test those who come; a single shout must cause the seas and mountains to darken.

Were it not for one who is a true son of the Dharma King, who would dare to tread upon his gate in ordinary circumstances? [The Master] replies: "For now, proceed slowly. [The student] advances and says: "Only..."

"Just as Śākyamuni Buddha spent forty-nine years speaking horizontally and vertically, yet could never exhaustively explain the matter to its very bottom—how will the Abbot Zen Master bestow [this teaching] tonight?

He replied, "I still feel it is too little. The questioner pressed further, "If there were no such eye for selecting the Buddha, how could the winds of our school have reached the present day? The Master picked up his staff and said, "This very thing is virtue."
The mountain staff. *Thump.* This alone is Linji’s shout. A clever fellow, before it has even been raised, seizes it in a single pull.
The water flows cold from the edge of the rock; the wind comes fragrant through the flowers.
If this is not yet so, I shall trouble this staff once more: borrowing Deshan’s nostrils, I shall let Linji vent his breath. *Thump.*
"Strike! A vajra-jewel sword. (He strikes once. "A lion crouching on the ground. (He strikes once. "The probing pole and the shadow-grass.
Is this single shout used as a shout, or is it not used as a shout? Is it the same as the three previous shouts, or is it different? If you say they are the same...
"Master Linji has still not been willing to nod his head. If you say they are different, how can you avoid being pierced through the nostrils by the old fellow Deshan all at once?
After all, how far apart are the nostrils of these two great elders, Deshan and Linji, from that which cannot be fully expressed even in forty-nine years of teaching?
He then leaned on his staff and said again, "Since we honor the lineage of the Śākyas..."
One must examine the teaching style of the Xu Shaomen lineage and scrutinize the ancestral school with precision. What kind of standard is this?
Have you not seen how Linji struck Huangbo three times and was beaten sixty times with a staff, as if it were merely a brush made of thistle?

And have you not seen how Deshan attained sudden enlightenment at Longtan’s place when the paper candle was extinguished, saying: "Exhaust all profound dialectics; it is like placing a single hair upon..."
The Great Void exhausts the pivotal mechanisms of the world, like a single drop cast into a vast abyss.

These two great elders may truly be said to have exhausted the marrow and bones of a thousand sages and penetrated the source of ten thousand dharmas; they have left their fragrance for future generations and established enduring models for the monastic community.
Those who study the Way today must also possess a measure of the "sinews of the eye" to see through the ancient ones' failures.
Only at this point of deficiency can one begin to attain it. If you can perceive this breach, you will see Huangbo and Longtan;
though this may seem like a golden-winged garuḍa cleaving the sea to seize and swallow the dragon, it nonetheless fails to avoid the treatment of a dead horse.

Linji and Deshan—though they do not depart from their present state and stride alone across the Great Square—they nevertheless abandon the long for the short and bury their own spiritual brilliance. To truly claim the hundred... [is impossible].
The World-Honored Master was not yet present at the gate of the Dharma Hall;
he would not have spoken of whether one has seen through it or not, for all such talk remains upon the crown of others' heads—the words of those who merely discharge their excrement.

Now that we are gathered here for a brief moment, Reverend Qin, I cannot help but borrow the majestic radiance of the Elder in the Hall to overturn the seas and mountains and shatter the great void. I must do so!
Everyone, take this as evidence. Although the King’s decree is most strict, how could one possibly jostle for position or snatch away the market?
This morning is the first day of the ninth month; the gong was struck for seated meditation. The Head Seat is called the "exemplar.

Yet perhaps there is but one person, or half a person—a Bodhisattva newly resolved in mind—who wishes to investigate and grasp this Way, yet has not yet found a point of entry, nor a place to set hand or foot. Or...
If one's practice has intervals and fails to achieve continuity, or if one experiences a slight sense of joy but no longer applies the whip to seek authentic awakening;
or if one has already found the gate of awakening but becomes deluded by that very awakening, such that the shadows and lights cannot be shed, thereby obstructing right knowledge and vision.
Some are shrouded by superior and exquisite pleasures, falling into the deep pit of liberation from which they cannot turn back;
others, regarding the various conditions and opportunities of the past and present, find them meaningful and fit for consumption, calculating each one until they can put them into practice.
That which is meaningless and difficult to chew upon cannot be analyzed or resolved.

Or, because of various strange words, wondrous phrases, profound principles, and mysterious texts, they remain as obstructions within the field of the eight consciousnesses and cannot be cast out; this is called "poisonous dregs entering the heart.
It is like oil mixed into flour, from which it can never be extracted. Now, if you wish to penetrate from top to bottom in a single turn, [you must act accordingly].
To turn it over, you must take a single ancient koan that is devoid of intellectual meaning and confront it as if it were an enemy;
only when you have truly been knocked flat on your face will you succeed. If you have not yet attained this realization, you will not.

Even if you were to travel on foot until the very ends of heaven and earth, and exhaustively memorize every word and phrase, opening your shop in spring and autumn like one selling "wolf-and-tiger" medicine, it would only increase your frivolous discourse and deceive future generations.
As for that single stroke beneath your own robe which is not worth half a coin, you have ultimately never touched upon it. If you truly wish to encounter it suddenly—
Severed! *Bò-dì-zhé-dǐ-hàn*. The eyes are fixed and still; speech is held with restraint. At every step, one departs from mud and water;
one sheds all habitual molds and traps. At all places and at all times, it is simply this state of total evenness and tranquility. How can it be otherwise?
"Life after life, they are fierce and arrogant; 'tsha tsha sa sa. They claim, 'I am without rival under heaven.
This is what is called the ninety-six types of heterodox paths from the Western Heaven. They boast of their intellectual understanding and cast aspersions upon the sages and worthies.
As for the Way of our Buddhas and Patriarchs, they are worlds apart from it. If you are a person of right cause and sincere resolve, do not be deceived by this."
It is sown within the soil of dust and rubble, overflowing from the source of the mind. One must believe that beneath the True Lineage lies the wondrous essence of the direct, single transmission;
only then can it be attained. Take, for example, Zhaozhou’s single word "Mu" (無): it is truly a sharp, polished sword drawn from its scabbard.
This can shatter the mass of doubt, sever birth and death, empty all phenomena, and harmonize past and present.
It requires only those of keen faculties and superior wisdom who, upon being struck, immediately turn, and upon being prodded, immediately act.

Only then will they be able to share the same eyes and the same enjoyment as the old man Zhaozhou, reaching even to the essential point where the myriad distinctions are unified and the thousand variations are opened.

The Gate: it is entirely guest and entirely host; entirely essence and entirely function; entirely release and entirely gathering; entirely life and entirely death—and all of this does not lie outside of this.

If one’s spiritual capacity is dull and one cannot practice the alternation of exertion and relaxation, one must instead rouse the backbone of raw iron, sit upright upon the long couch, settle firmly upon a thick meditation cushion, and remain steadfast until the three hundred and sixty bones are fully engaged.
Section. Take the eighty-four thousand pores of the body and together with them, make them into a single "Mu" (無).

Clench both fists and strain both eyes; lift it up with a single pull, as if you were about to cut it in two. If you can spur yourself in this way and exert such effort, why worry that it will not become a complete whole?
Why worry that you will not reach the end? When you feel as though you cannot lift it, [you must redouble your resolve].
When you feel increasingly feverish and distressed—during that state of distress and when everything is dark and turbulent—you must let go entirely and release yourself.
Turn yourself around and walk a few paces on the spot; while walking, likewise apply the spur and exert effort in this way.
At that very moment, there will be a distinct shift in your spirit. Then, turn your body back onto the meditation cushion and stand upright.
As one sits, the interior of the chest becomes clear and still, like a silver mountain or an iron wall—a vast emptiness, a profound silence.
At this moment, where is there even a single thread of movement? Where is there even a single thread of difference? When one reaches this state...
One must not remain stuck here; rather, one must turn over and descend to the ground, as if walking while seated, and then again sit while walking.
When the day is insufficient, continue through the night; when the night is insufficient, continue until dawn.
Turning back and forth, lifting up and bringing down, before one knows it, suddenly one breaks through—like a poor man finding treasure. It is like...

Darkness meets the lamp; it is like clouds parting to reveal the sun, or a fire breaking out from the bottom of the water. Throughout the ocean of lands of the ten directions, this is the Great Perfect Mirror.
Throughout the ocean of lands of the ten directions, this is one's own self. This is called "passing the imperial examination with an empty mind.
It is seeing through to the face before one’s parents were born. If one explains the Great Dharma clearly, penetrating past and present, one fulfills the legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Profound! It is like entering the ocean; only then can one plant one's feet. Before one is even there, the vast waves reach the heavens and the great surges wash over the sun.
Where else could one go? One must by no means listen to those who say that "awakening" is merely a figurative expression. This matter has been perfectly manifest from the very beginning;
it requires nothing more than a single smile to know where to return. If it were simply a matter of cause and effect, what need would there be for the riddle-beating across the wall?
Blue, yellow, red, and white; long, short, square, and round—ultimately, you have never personally seen them.

When someone places them before you, what is clearly a rare and wondrous treasure you instead call a piece of rubble, brick, or tile; and what is clearly a piece of rubble, brick, or tile you instead call a rare and wondrous treasure.
Furthermore, do not listen to people saying that practicing Chan is fundamentally a matter of peace and bliss.

This is the Dharma-gate. Therein, there is much coming and going, much bustle and clamor; one need only silently maintain the alertness of mindfulness, and after a long time, one will naturally accord with it.
This is called "soaking a stone in dead water"—there is never a moment of awakening or movement.
Furthermore, one must not listen to those who say that this single word "Mu" (No) is merely a tethering stake for a donkey; one simply needs to maintain it.
It comes and settles right before you. Grasp it firmly and bind this single thought. When the thought becomes matured, you will naturally arrive home.
Yet, little do you realize that this single thought is like a flickering flame or a trickling stream;
in the blink of an eye, it has traveled a thousand miles and ten thousand leagues. Were it not for a sudden, total letting go, how could you ever grasp it firmly or bind it?

One attains abiding. Furthermore, one must not listen to people saying that it is enough to grasp at the place where sounds are heard and forms are seen, or to take responsibility for the places of turning, moving, bowing, and looking up.
To speak with the mouth is to hit upon it; to move a step is to tread upon it.

At the gates of the six sense organs, there is a single ray of divine light that never ceases day or night. This is called the root of birth and death, a mass of deluded karmic consciousness. Hurry! Hurry!
One must cut it into three pieces. Furthermore, one must not listen to what others say. From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established.
Originally, there have been no mountains, rivers, or the great earth; no light or darkness, no form or emptiness; no Buddhas and no patriarchs; no sentient beings;
no ordinary people and no sages; no good and no evil; no going and no coming; no birth and no death. This is called "vast openness."
To utterly deny cause and effect is to wander aimlessly and invite calamity. Furthermore, one must not listen to those who claim to "sit and cut off the master" or "not fall into the second view.
Wearing clothes and eating food, one does not borrow another's power. Mountains are mountains; waters are waters; monks are monks;
laypeople are laypeople. This is the Dharma abiding in its own position; the characteristics of the world are eternally present. This may be so.

"It seems so, yet it is not yet so. As stated above, all of these are self-created obstacles, self-generated despondency, self-abandonment and self-neglect, and self-inflicted injury and cruelty—pathological conditions that no physician can reach their root.
Only by taking a single dose of this "miraculous elixir that transforms the bones" and breaking into a profuse sweat can one thereafter truly know whether one is afflicted by cold, heat, or hunger.
Enough of this talk of injury and satiety; it is all simply the field of great rest, great repose, and great peace and bliss.
To transform eighty-four thousand ailments into eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates—this body is the ailment, these weeds are the medicine.
It can kill all people, and it can also sustain all people. Adjusting the dosage according to the occasion and applying the remedy according to the specific diagnosis, one [attains liberation].
It all depends on me. If the foundation is not firm and the original vital energy (*yuanqi*) is insufficient, do not let others administer even a single grain of castor oil (*bādou*);
you will immediately feel it erupt throughout your entire body, your face will turn black, your vision will blur, and in an instant, your very life will vanish without a trace.

If one were a person who could discern safety from peril and distinguish between good and ill fortune, then whether it be *amṛta* (clarified butter) or poison, I would overturn it for you face-to-face;
within a single hair’s breadth, there would be another path leading to the heavens.

Nowadays, everything is merely a matter of oral and written transmission—corrupt medical texts—and not a single person is seen who possesses the wondrous skill of divine mastery; such things only mislead people.
There are many such instances. Often, people point to seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; they take the raising of eyebrows or the blinking of eyes as their own self.
Furthermore, they cite "mind itself is Buddha" and the passage about preaching and listening to the Dharma right before one's eyes—this vivid, solitary clarity—as proof.
Only then do they raise the case of the wind moving or the banner moving, or "it is neither the wind moving nor the banner moving," and then call this very thing [the self].
These are established as koans for beginners, intended to lead you here to refine and clarify your insight (*jìndì*) and to excavate the fundamental source.
Subsequently, he again brings up cases such as "The Cypress Tree," "Three Pounds of Flax," and "A Dry Shit-stick," which are called single-headed and superficial koans;

these are meant to teach you how to recognize the *huátó* (the critical phrase) at the very moment you open your mouth. After that, he further cites the cases of Xuefeng’s "Xuansha was not yet thorough" and Zhaozhou’s...
Cases such as that of Old Lady Kanpō are called the "touchstone" and also the "black beans for changing one's eyes.
Then, cases such as Baizhang’s Wild Fox and the Woman Emerging from Samādhi are called the "pivot of the School" and the "tongs for seizing dragons and striking phoenixes.
Finally, cases such as Mazu’s Single Shout and Yantou’s Final Word are cited.
This is called the "claws and fangs" that transcend [the ordinary], the very "nose" of the patch-robed monk (*śramaṇa*).

Even the ancient "frozen sores" of the past—when it comes to their essential means of bestowing compassion and benefiting beings—all possess the mold from the printing block, the pattern cast forth for you to excavate from the beginning and annotate from the beginning.
To fit this pattern perfectly is what is called "clarifying the Great Dharma" and penetrating through.
Throughout antiquity and the present, people fail to realize that, fortunately, one is originally a single, pure crystal flask.

For no reason, they have poured into it a vast amount of chaotic filth. Furthermore, they do not know that from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old down to all the elder monks throughout the world, they share but a single tongue;
sometimes they employ a single pivot, yet it manifests in a thousand ways.
The myriad functions are simultaneously fulfilled. At times, he utters a single phrase, and a thousand or ten thousand phrases converge upon the same track.
At times, he points to a thousand or ten thousand phrases, yet they are but a single function. At times, he brings forth a thousand or ten thousand functions, yet they are but a single phrase.

It reaches the point where heaven and earth are shaken, covering the sky and veiling the earth—like the spark struck from flint, like a flash of lightning. Whether one can grasp it or not, it remains so.
Even if you were to attain it, you would still not have avoided losing your body and life; where would there be room for you to look on with your own intent, or for your mind to settle upon it?

Furthermore, how could this be like the village scholar of the world who is taught the Elementary Learning and then proceeds from the "Great Men" to read the *Analects*, *Mencius*, *Book of Poetry*, and *Book of Changes* all at once?
If it were so, what need would there have been for nine years of facing the wall? To stand [in such practice]—
The snow reaches the waist. Simply transmit it thus; simply learn it thus, and then let it rest. You should know that this matter is a world-transcending dharma (*lokottara-dharma*);
one must possess world-transcending eyes and a world-transcending capacity to take it up upon one shoulder before it can be attained.

If you merely twist and mold it as you go along, measure and weigh it as you go along, and analyze it as you go along—relying on what is called the emotional consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to gauge the Tathāgata—you will never succeed.
How inconceivable! The great ocean of Perfect Enlightenment is such that even if one were to take a firefly and attempt to burn Mount Sumeru with it, it could never set it ablaze.
Even if you were to stuff yourself full of leftovers and rancid rice, would there be even a single grain of use in it?
Could it ever deceive anyone else? Even if it could deceive others, could it ever deceive oneself? Even...
You may deceive yourself, but can you deceive the lanterns and the pillars?
Since you cannot deceive them, you cannot avoid being laughed at from the sidelines by the myriad phenomena of the universe. Take Master Qin, for instance; tonight, he acts just like this.
The mouth is parched and the tongue is parched with agitation; they speak in a jumble of seven ways and eight paths. Tell me, can you even manage to produce this one laugh?
If you say you cannot, you will inevitably be counted among the ninety-six types of heterodox schools in the Western Heavens.
If you say you can, alas, there are bystanders watching. Now tell me, where are these bystanders? It is late at night; I have stood here for a long time. I prostrate myself.
Please take this to heart.
After entering the room, he spoke to the assembly at large: "Brothers, remain here for a moment.
We shall gather for a short while so that I may twist your nostrils and split open the great void. Although it is like gouging a sore from good flesh, the blade is nonetheless made of iron."
Do you yet know that within a single phrase there are three mysteries (*xuán*), and within each mystery there are three essentials (*yào*)?

Furthermore, do you yet know that within the guest (*bīn*) there is the host (*zhǔ*), and within the host there is the guest? At times the guest is entirely the host; at times the host is entirely the guest?
Furthermore, do you know that within killing there is life, and within life there is killing? Is it ever the case that total killing is life, or that total life is killing?
Furthermore, do you know that when the mouth opens, it is not upon the tongue? Furthermore, do you know that one hand lifts while the other hand presses down?
If you cannot clearly discern these points, the distinction between the ordained and the laity will not be realized, and you shall not escape being seen as a mere man.
To say "this is right" when it is right, and to say "this is wrong" when it is wrong—this is precisely what is called "the short man watching the play," following others up and down.
How could one know that within the green cloth curtain there was, all along, someone present?
As for this talk, let alone those who have not yet gained their own ground and cannot grasp it; even those ten practitioners of Chan who wear the green cloth robes [would not understand].
Five pairs. It is like swallowing a jujube whole; do not speak further of using the conscious intellect to calculate it.

Those who merely follow what is passed down by mouth and ear give rise to interpretations based on words and engage in forced analysis with every phrase; this is certain. You must know that this is a sublime excellence beyond categories and transcending the mundane.

One must not engage in deliberation or conjecture; it does not involve seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. Furthermore, one must know that everyone is fully endowed with it and each individual is perfectly accomplished.
It is only because, throughout immeasurable eons, we have been tossed about by birth and death and obscured by the karmic consciousness of ignorance.

It is obscured; it cannot manifest before you, nor can it be utilized. Now, if you wish to turn this over once and for all prior to the time of King Majestic Sound (Vaiśravaṇa-rāja), you must have faith that this very point is truly an inherent possession of your own, certainly not something obtained from others.
Only then will you exhaust the body born of your parents and the vital energy received from Heaven and Earth.
Combine these into a single blade of sharp, piercing sword and cut your own solitary life-force into two pieces, casting them down over a precipice ten thousand fathoms high.
Only when the myriad phenomena of the universe have utterly subsided into stillness can it be called "passing the imperial examination with an empty mind" or "the radiance of the ocean-seal.
If you depart from this, then even if you should manage to penetrate the matter until your belly is full, it is of no avail.
I have constructed a single cloth bag. On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, I shall inevitably find myself flustered and frantic, like a crab falling into boiling water.
When I was under the guidance of Wuzhun and Chijue, I had a friend who frequently offered a word or two that became as famous as minced meat on a skewer;
he also fully understood the underlying intent in the ancients' indirect strikes and silent blows. However—

This person had never performed any personal cultivation upon the meditation cushion. Later, he served as a library director (*tsang-chu*) in various regions, where his temperament was haughty and his conduct superior to his peers.
One day, because he was embroiled in several frivolous lawsuits and could not resolve the complications, he was defeated by others.
Consequently, his resentment festered; he vomited blood and fell ill, from which he did not recover. At the moment of his death, he was suddenly struck by a thousand... [the text here is incomplete].
He experienced myriad sufferings; though he sought death, he could not die. Whenever he saw friends come to inquire after his illness, he would say: "I practice Chan.
Throughout my life, I have never applied myself to the work upon the meditation cushion. I did not believe there was a gate of enlightenment, but merely focused on the written texts.
I presumed that the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs ended with this. Today, having arrived here, not even a single..."
It is of no use. I urge you all: when practicing Chan, do not be like me. You must perform solid, foundational work before you can succeed.
Having said this, tears fell once more. This is the very appearance of one who does not believe there is a gate to enlightenment.
In death, one knows not where one goes; in birth, one knows not whence one comes. What is called the matter of birth and death is of great importance.
Impermanence is swift: in the blink of an eye, it is already the next life. Suddenly, when this single breath ceases, the path ahead is vast and empty; one knows not where one will go.

You have entered the belly of a donkey or a horse; you see nothing at all. You lot, beginners and latecomers, why do you not take advantage of your physical strength and vigor to strike through to the bottom?
Here, on this solitary peak and highest summit, is the place of the forge and bellows; it is the warmth of the monastic grove, where everything is spontaneously present.
The offerings from the Hall of Fragrant Accumulation are sublime. If you do not strike through to the bottom right here—how will you ever do so?
To depart [from this path] may be called betraying the Buddhas and Patriarchs, betraying the donors, betraying one's teachers and friends, and betraying oneself.
If, for even a single moment, one is not upright, and stumbles or falls, then if one does not understand for oneself, every grain of rice and every stalk of vegetable broth [will be wasted].
"You must all use oxen to pull plows and drag harrows to repay your debts before you can attain liberation.

Have you not seen how, during the summer months, many deceased monks were each cremated until they became a single heap of ashes and sent to rest within the Three Pagodas? Where do they dwell and establish their lives now?
Do you know? If you do not even know this, is it not the case that you do not know where you go when you die? This is what is called the 'greatness of death.'"
Right now, as your eyes blink, right here, I ask you about the countenance prior to the birth of your parents—a state where one cannot open one's mouth.
Is this not what is called "not knowing where one comes from at birth," which is termed "the greatness of birth"? Indeed, the matter of birth and death is truly great.
You must treat this as a single matter, a truly great and momentous affair. You must straighten your spine of raw iron and seek instruction until you understand it clearly.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, do not allow your mind to be distracted; do not remain aimlessly drifting and wasting your time in vain.
You must forge it into a single piece of unity. You must ensure that this very thought-moment is free from even a thread of...

Only when there is not even a hair’s breadth of interruption can it be attained. In ancient times, those who esteemed the Way regarded the reading of sutras and the study of teachings as a distracted use of the mind;
how much more so for you, who from the time you rise each morning do nothing but pursue this and that, flitting about like a restless monkey, busying yourselves with worldly affairs?
Furthermore, the ancients also said that practicing Chan and studying the Way is a distracted use of the mind. Since practicing Chan and studying the Way is already considered a distraction...
"You apply your mind. Yet I tell you to apply your mind there! [He lets out a shout. Inside the Hanyuan Hall, why must one further ask for Chang'an?

It is simply because your single thought of seeking has not ceased; you have abandoned your present livelihood and yet desire to ascend to heaven or enter the earth, seeking a separate way of life and seeking the Buddha-dharma elsewhere. Therefore, you exhaust all your wiles and suffer to the utmost."

Through diligent effort, one’s delusions may only increase further. If you can suddenly and directly cease this state of restless seeking for a single moment, then all phenomena will be quiescent in their very essence.
Yet all phenomena will continue to blaze forth as before. Walking is fine; sitting is fine. Wearing clothes and eating food—this is none other than yourself.
Mountains are green and waters are blue; nights are dark and days are bright; dullness and distraction, birth-and-death and nirvana—all are [one].
This is one's own home. One sports freely therein, attaining the Dharma-gate of great mastery. There is not a single dharma to be discarded, nor a single dharma to be grasped.
Both Buddhas and sentient beings are merely provisional names; they possess no substantial reality whatsoever.
Nevertheless, you must also have your own eyes opened, and with a cold laugh, know that the source is already within your own house, right in front of the main hall.

Only then can one attain the Great Seat. There are some individuals—perhaps even half-persons—who open their mouths but do not know the path of speech, and who step forward without knowing the difference between high and low ground.
Even if they wish to ascend the master’s hall and enter the master’s chamber, it is doubtful they will succeed. Now, the great matter cannot be entrusted to you;

It enters right into the eye. The mountains, rivers, and the great earth; light and darkness, form and emptiness—are these not the Buddha? Are they not the Dharma? The movement of the wind and the rising of dust;
the cawing of crows and the chirping of magpies—are these not the Buddha? Are they not the Dharma? The succession of the four seasons; the flourishing and withering of the myriad things;
the sun shining when the sky clears and the ground becoming damp when rain falls—are these not the Buddha? Are they not the Dharma? Even unto the ultimate truth...
Is it not the Buddha and the Dharma when one speaks of Prajñā, Bodhi, Nirvāṇa, ignorance, afflictions, deluded thoughts, and inversions;
or when one walks, stands, sits, lies down, bends, turns, stoops, or looks up? This is merely the "daily tea and rice" learned within the monasteries of all quarters;
what connection does it have [to the truth]? Since there is no connection, is it perhaps the clay shrine or the molded image?
Are the yellow scrolls and red axes the Buddha? Are they the Dharma? Furthermore, is it the "mind itself" or "not mind," both being and non-being, half-closed and half-open?
Is that the Buddha? Is that the Dharma? Furthermore, is it the "three pounds of hemp," the "dry dung pellet," or the "cypress tree in the courtyard"?
Is that the Buddha? Is that the Dharma? Furthermore, is it Avalokiteśvara? Or is it buying sesame cakes with cash? Let go...
The origin of the hand is originally a steamed bun. A frog leaps up into the heavens; an earthworm suddenly crosses the Eastern Sea. Is this Buddha? Is this Dharma?
Furthermore, is it not the entirety of the seventeen hundred cases, where host and guest alternate and the mechanisms of life and death unfold?
Is it not the Great Canon, with its five periods and eight teachings, and the principles of the provisional and the real? Is this Buddha? Is this Dharma? This very thing—
Furthermore, what connection can there be with these old, frozen sores from all directions—nothing but the vomited drool and spittle of wild foxes?
Since there is no connection, is it this very mouth chattering and these eyes blinking right now that constitute the Buddha or the Dharma?
This is called beating a bag of ignorance and playing with the vapors of rice and gruel; within this total lack of connection, there is yet more.

For what reason? These ten individuals, five pairs of them, are like those who move by leaning on a fence or feeling their way along a wall; they lack any freedom of action.

If you act in this manner, you will inevitably create a duality. When such duality is not yet overcome, every movement and every stillness fails to prevent you from splitting your daily life into two separate parts.
Thus, it is impossible for you to realize that waking and sleeping are one and the same, or that birth and death are without interval.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, you cannot avoid having half of your practice as Buddhist Dharma and half as worldly dharma, which remain in mutual opposition.

there is that which is right and that which is wrong; and yet there is also that which neither hears nor sees, and is neither right nor wrong.
To try to carve out a space for one's own enjoyment and attempt to unify it into a single whole is impossible.
Furthermore, this very talk of "unifying into a single whole" is often misunderstood;
people imagine there is some object right here before them, upon which they must exert effort and apply power to achieve this unification. Little do they realize that you need only—
Forgetting knowledge and forgetting awareness, severing seeing and severing hearing, one naturally becomes a single piece.
Yet, from this very place, one plays freely and unrestrainedly, emerging in seven ways and disappearing in eight, manifesting great potential and revealing great function.
Thus, from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past down to all people throughout the entire earth, their very lives and natures are entirely contained within this vast, sky-reaching net. At times...
To hold fast is permissible; to teach you to abide is also permissible. At times, to let go is permissible; to teach you to depart is also permissible.
At times, to teach you to live is permissible; to teach you to die is also permissible. At times, to speak to you of right and wrong is also permissible.

Sometimes it is said to you that there is a Way, or that there is no Way; even when one reaches the point of dismantling the framework of the leaks, shifting the constellations, and taking south for north—all of this does not depart from this very single point.

That you have not yet reached this state is because your emotions obstruct your wisdom and your conceptualizations alter its essence, causing you to abandon your own manifest perfection and cast away your boundless vitality.
Yet, within the realm of what is seen and heard, and the sphere of sound and form, you wish to arbitrarily establish boundaries and confine yourself in narrowness.

As soon as there is even the slightest transgression of these borders or encroachment upon these domains, you find the title deeds unclear and unable to act as the rightful master. This has been so from the time of the Buddhas and Patriarchs above.
That which has been passed down from father to son through successive generations—this ancient and modern world, overgrown with brambles and weeds—is what is truly pitiable.
When the Venerable Qin arrived here, he simply did not shrink from toil or hardship; he took your hand and plowed the ground until the very bottom.
He gave a shout and said: "This alone is the ancient and modern world. This alone is the ancient and modern sun and moon."
This alone is it. This alone is the ancestral legacy of all Buddhas and Patriarchs. This alone is the father’s deed of conveyance.
This alone is one’s own livelihood. This alone is the seed of ignorance. This alone is where brambles and thickets intermingle. This alone is when the rice is fragrant and the fruit is ripe.
Before a single shout has been uttered, before a single thought has arisen, and before a single speck of dust has been established—right here, take a single step.
Treading upon it, the myriad phenomena stand arrayed; at once, they fold their hands in reverence. What more need be said? The four directions are clearly demarcated;
karma returns to its original master. It reaches the point where the entire ocean of lands throughout the great trichiliocosm, all ten billion worlds, is one’s own self.
Exhausting the vastness of kalpas, the ten billion Buddhas and patriarchs are one’s descendants. Even unto the transformation of mulberry fields into the blue sea, [it is all encompassed]. Shorten...
Ten thousand generations are but a single moment; such is the natural law, and there is nothing extraordinary about it.

If you do not reach this state, how can you be said to have realized the Great Dharma and penetrated past and present? Furthermore, how could you distinguish between dragons and snakes, or capture tigers and rhinoceroses?
If you do not possess the resolute spirit that does not blink when killing people, you will inevitably be dragged into the realms of the aggregates and the four elements by them.
Furthermore, it would not be otherwise; today three, tomorrow four—once winter sets in.
If your feverish energy rises for only half the time and your faith remains divided between belief and doubt, how can there ever be a moment of accomplishment?
How can there ever be news of reaching the destination? You must exert yourself regardless of your own life, charging straight forward.

Only by seizing the head of Yan Liang amidst a hundred thousand troops can you issue commands over all under heaven. If you remain merely timid and hesitant, you will bring only disaster upon yourself.
Disaster after disaster, omen after omen. Searching east and investigating west, looking under the ground for a needle—what does this accomplish?

Even if you were suddenly to see through a single phrase and experience a moment of joy, and then review it from beginning to end, thinking you have finally understood it all, by the time tomorrow or the day after comes, do not let yourself run into a single phrase that you cannot penetrate.
"Too late! Wait until it is brought up from the very beginning and you take one look; then neither of these will do either. Furthermore, listen here:

chew on this from east to west, reconcile it within the *songgu* (ancient verses), investigate within the *songgu*, search through the *Biyanji* (Blue Cliff Record), listen with your ears, and probe within your belly.
Suddenly, when you strike upon it, you will penetrate this single phrase, and you will rejoice once more."
The superior student further thinks that everything has been fully resolved.
Suddenly, when things are not quite right, some witless fellow comes along and makes a slash with his hand before you; yet you cannot penetrate it, and even the seal is no longer correct.
There is nothing else. It is simply because your knot of doubt has not been broken; you have always been wandering within the realm of feeling, intellect, and consciousness.
When you reach a point where the paths of thought no longer function, it suddenly stands before you like a silver mountain or an iron wall.
Whether you face it horizontally or vertically, there is no way out. At this moment, you must take a step back and turn it over completely, casting it aside.

Only then can you succeed from behind. If you push forward step by step, press against it step by step, pierce it step by step, and bore through it step by step—even if you manage to find a slight crack or fissure, what can you do?
A silver mountain and an iron wall remain right before your face; you cannot dissolve them, and yet you do not even see them.
Master Baiyun Yuan said: "From of old, there has been left behind a single word or half a phrase."

For those who have not yet penetrated it, it is like a silver mountain and an iron wall. But once you have penetrated it, you realize that your own self is precisely that silver mountain and iron wall.
Now tell me: is it Baiyun’s statement that is correct, or is it the Venerable Qin’s statement that is correct?
If you can see through this point, then these one thousand seven hundred cases—these miscellaneous household utensils—will all at once be threaded together by you like a string of pearls.
It has already been cast behind you. Should it be otherwise, you will inevitably encounter silver mountains and iron walls right before your eyes, unable to digest them.
At such a time, which one is the Venerable One’s own self? (He lets out a shout. "The sword has long since departed.

May you dwell in ten thousand blessings. During the summer months, I was mistakenly favored by the Abbot with the appointment to hang the plaque; I am deeply ashamed that my talent is so meager and that I am utterly unworthy of this office.

Only, as the weather is bitterly cold, I lead this great assembly with a sense of trepidation and perspiration. Here is a four-line verse: "Awake and asleep, it is one and the same."

If even a hair’s breadth of view arises at this point, you will once again be lost in the vagueness of crossing a foreign land.
The Universal Discourse at Bao’en Temple in Huzhou: "Seventy monks from thirty-three prefectures, with donkey jaws and horse foreheads, are loathed by all.

then you will see that those who put on their robes and eat their meals are none other than yourselves—just like the cawing of crows and the chirping of magpies."

From the beginning, this was not an external object. Even if one’s faculty of faith is dull and fails to turn back after three attempts, that is simply because you lacked the seeds of spiritual potential in your past lives;
it cannot be blamed on Xueyan. It is just like the butcher Guang'e at the assembly of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, who cast down his butcher’s blade and said, "I am counted among the thousand Buddhas.
