A single "is" and a single "is not"—these two characters are perched upon the crown of the forehead. Go everywhere to verify that old staff at the corner of the meditation seat.
For one such as this, there is a place for you to dwell. You must practice authentically; you must realize authentically.
King Yama does not fear your many words. I urge you, you latecomers and beginners: why do you not take advantage of [this time]?
With a body strong and vigorous, go straight forward. If you retreat, it is for your own sake; strike until you have thoroughly penetrated it.
Do not merely be indolent and drifting, or get caught up in "this" and "that," or enter into the sack of antiquities.

You must truly rouse the backbone of raw iron and, upon the meditation cushion, crush everything to pieces in a single squeeze, until even empty space breaks into a sweat and the great earth sinks flat.

Only then can you attain it. If you do not yet possess this power, you must, during the twelve periods of the day—whether walking or sitting, putting on clothes or eating, or even when defecating or urinating—single-mindedly hold up a single ancient koan devoid of intellectual meaning.
Like Mount Sumeru, let it settle squarely within your eighty-four thousand pores and three hundred and sixty joints.

Within the joints of the bones, mind follows mind in succession and thought follows thought in continuity. Suddenly, at a point where effort reaches its limit, one turns everything over from the very bottom.
Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, this is the great field of liberation; this is the great treasury of radiant light.
One may then join hands with the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and patriarchs of the past, appearing and disappearing together, sporting within that realm as one pleases.
"Could one possibly conceive of placing a potter’s wheel upon the palm of one's hand? Last evening, the assembly of monks brought incense up here;

after they had finished their prostrations, they wished to request that you preach for the sake of the community at large. The head of the assembly stepped forward and said: 'We are ignorant and dull-witted, possessing no knowledge whatsoever.
We humbly hope that you will not withhold your compassion, but will reveal the primary truth (paramārtha-satya), so that we may attain an entrance.'"
As for this matter, if we discuss the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it is precisely that one must realize there is nothing to be known.
Why then do you insist on placing a head upon your head, or seeking out the ox while already riding it? Let me ask you: when you eat, do you still have to ask others for the mouth with which to eat?

Directly cutting off the heads of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* Buddhas—like a layman being appointed as a high minister, or ascending to immortality on level ground—there is no second person and no second thought.

it is the sword that cuts through the roots of the dream-like cycle of birth and death for you; it is the mirror that reflects the myriad differences of the past and present.
It matters only that, before the word is even raised, you turn yourself around with a single leap and cast it away to the other side.
On the other side, one reaches a state of pure, unadorned clarity—eight holes and seven gaps where the Great Function manifests, leaving no room for fixed rules.
Nevertheless, for me to speak thus is like digging a pond in the great ocean or nailing a stake into empty space;
compared to the matters of the True Lineage, it is far, far removed. What, then, are the matters of the True Lineage? It would be better to doze off at night.
Sleep well.
Hundreds of thousands of diverse streams all return to the great ocean; hundreds of thousands of diverse dharmas all return to this school.

Like the sky universally covering all, like the earth universally supporting all, the warbling of swallows and the singing of orioles together perform the Tathāgata’s true reality (*tathatā*); the green mountains and blue waters solely clarify it.

The pure Dharma-body—if one were a superior person of outstanding character, they would have immediately shouted to disperse the assembly, overturned the meditation seat, and given this old monk a sound beating, saying, "Do not further mislead future generations by blinding their eyes to come!
Would that not have brought joy to one's entire life? If, however, you merely clasp your hands over your chest and wait submissively for instructions, you cannot avoid citing a few [words]:

This is the tangle of rotten weeds; it drags people along with it. Have you not seen how when Master Yongjia first visited the Sixth Patriarch, he went to Caoxi, circumambulated the meditation seat three times, struck his staff once, and stood there resolutely.
The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa possesses three thousand dignified demeanors and eighty thousand subtle practices. How can you give rise to such great arrogance? Yongjia—

[Daowu] said, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. Yongjia said, "Why not realize non-arising and comprehend that there is no swiftness? The Master said, "It is so, it is so.
Yongjia then adjusted his demeanor, performed a prostration, and after a short while took his leave. The Master said, "Why have you returned so quickly? Yongjia replied, "Fundamentally..."
"If it is not moving by itself, how could there be speed? The Patriarch said, "Who knows that it is not moving? Yongjia said, "The benevolent one simply gives rise to discrimination.
The Patriarch said, "You have grasped the meaning of non-arising very well. Yongjia said, "How can non-arising have any meaning?"
The Patriarch said, "If there is no intention, who is it that discriminates? Yongjia said, "Discrimination, too, is not intention.
The Patriarch said, "Excellent, excellent! Stay for one night. From then on, the monastic community referred to him as "One-Night Enlightenment" (Yisujue).

Brothers, we are all alike in setting out from home to travel beyond our borders, seeking teachers and investigating the Way; yet among them, Yongjia was exceptional. Observe his every movement—his every...
Silence. One word, one silence—from that moment on, he covered heaven and earth, illuminating the past and soaring through the present.

Furthermore, observe him as he circumambulated the meditation seat three times, struck his staff once, and stood there with majestic composure. What kind of spirit is this? Without cause, the Sixth Patriarch said:
"A śramaṇa possesses the three thousand dignified postures and eighty thousand subtle practices; how can you give rise to such great arrogance?"
"How greatly you have been humbled! Yongjia said, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. A flushed face is not as good as straightforward speech.
The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize non-arising and comprehend that there is no swiftness? I thought there might be something extraordinary here."
Yongjia said, "The essence is fundamentally unborn; to realize it is fundamentally without haste. It is a waste to labor over analytical distinctions.
The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is. This is the 'winter melon seal'. Yongjia then composed his demeanor and prostrated. After a short while, he took his leave.
Now tell me, how does this differ from striking the monk's staff once and standing upright? The Patriarch said, "Why do you return so quickly? And yet...
This circulated among the world. Yongjia said, "Since it is fundamentally not moving, how could there be speed?
He spoke a few words of principle. The Patriarch said, "Who knows it is not moving? and let out a shout. Yongjia said, "The benevolent one creates distinctions himself; you are quite stubborn.
The Patriarch said, "You have grasped the meaning of non-arising very well," yet this was merely a "winter melon seal. Yongjia said, "There is none."
"Does Sheng have any intention? From beginning to end, he has recognized only a single peg. The Patriarch said, "If there is no intention, who is it that makes distinctions?
Why do you not give him his rightful fodder? Yongjia said, "Even making distinctions is not an intention. [The Patriarch] struck thirty blows; even one blow would not have sufficed.
The Patriarch said, "Excellent, excellent! Stay for one more night. What a great Patriarch! He let him pass.
Yongjia has already realized it. Now, you brothers, when you cross the threshold of others' gates, you may indeed say, "The matter of birth and death is great;
impermanence is swift. Yet, as soon as you enter the Sangha hall, you are immediately changed by a bowl of five-flavor soup, which causes you to forget everything all at once.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, you are either busy with trivialities or...

Thus it is said that the seven paths become eight. Even if there were one person or half a person who truly took this as a single matter upon the meditation cushion, they would be either in a state of dullness or distraction;
how could they ever have for even a moment or a brief instant the occasion of Yongjia circling the bed three times, striking his staff once, and standing firm? And how could they ever...
To know is to realize that the essence is fundamentally unborn and that the source is fundamentally without speed; yet how could one ever have known this? Even discrimination is not of the mind.
As days pass and months deepen, one cannot avoid falling into the ranks of those who merely consume their daily gruel and rice. Therefore it is said:
"Since you honor the lineage of Śākyamuni, you must inherit the tradition of our school. Examine closely the primary source: what is its standard and character? One must truly arouse great courage.

Fierce! Establishing a great vow, disregarding peril and ruin, one moves straight forward, asking no more of life or death, of ignorance or affliction, of suchness or prajñā, of dullness or distraction. With a single stroke, everything is cut in two.
From the bare-boned ground, one leaps forth; from within the vast ocean, one turns over; upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Having first set foot upon it, one then single-mindedly raises the supreme seal of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Across the billion-fold mountains, rivers, and great earth;
throughout the billion-fold past and present; whether sages or ordinary beings, whether grass or trees—all are sealed and determined by this one seal.
Without leaving out even a hair’s breadth. He raises his whisk and says: "Look! Look! The seal-pattern is revealed.
With eyes discerning and hands skillful, if one seizes it once, one may let it come tumbling down and turning upside-down;

whether draped crosswise or vertically, whether god or ghost, whether heterodox or orthodox—it all receives a single stroke upon the face, leaving them no way to turn back and no door to escape. This is called the Sea.
The Seal Samādhi is also called the "Ocean-Seal Radiance. At such a time, one does not perceive birth and death, nor is one separated from nirvāṇa;
one does not perceive ignorance or afflictions, nor dullness and distraction, nor is one separated from true thusness or liberation, nor from prajñā or bodhi.
Can you still believe this? Once it has been placed within your grasp, there is no harm in bringing it forth. Face to face—[do so].
This single seal of the assembly breaks open the face-gates of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the three periods of time. It requires the lanterns and pillars to join in providing witness.
Is there such? Is there? If not, this mountain monk cannot help but borrow the words of Master Yongjia when he saw the Sixth Patriarch.
He strikes the ground once with his staff and draws a line, saying: "The seams of the brocade are opened; the authentic seal is brought forth and displayed universally for all people.
He strikes again: "The three essentials are revealed by the opening of the seal; though the vermilion dot is narrow, there is no room for hesitation—the host and guest are distinguished."
The Universal Discourse on the Incense Offering: Time passes swiftly and easily into old age; the fruit of existence is impermanent and rapid. Like dreams and illusions, it is not solid.

Is it not the case that the matter of birth and death is of the utmost gravity? A man of true power turns things over once and for all, until the great earth sinks into stillness, heaven and earth are revealed in their nakedness, the ten-thousand-mile long sky is free of even a speck of dust, and the myriad phenomena of the forested world—whether looking up, looking down, or turning—manifest as the total embodiment of reality.
This is the Great Treasury of Radiance. Buddhas and sentient beings enjoy it together, without the slightest difference.

It is only because emotions arise that wisdom is obstructed, and because conceptual thoughts transform that the essence becomes distinct. Thus, the four classes of noble ones and the six realms of ordinary beings transmigrate within the three realms;

amidst the good and evil destinies, they have no means of escape. Consequently, my predecessors, the Sages, exhausted themselves by casting off their precious and regal robes to don tattered and soiled garments, and [bestowed this teaching] upon us.
Thus, you share life and death; you come and go together. You dwell together within the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, wondrously luminous ocean of nature.

You open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; you manifest the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. You speak of non-existence and existence; you speak of "is" and "is not. You speak of emptiness and the provisional;

you speak of the expedient and the real. You speak of the orthodox and the partial; you speak of the One Vehicle, the Perfect and Sudden. This extends even to the separate transmission outside the teachings, where one employs the staff.
He utters shouts; he points to space and speaks of emptiness. He opens the mysterious gate of the Three Essentials and distinguishes the four kinds of critical examination.

Through the Five Ranks of Ruler and Subject, a single arrowhead pierces the three barriers. Two mouths have but one tongue. He clarifies the mind through form and reveals the principle through objects.
"Three pounds of flax," "a dry dung pellet," "the cypress tree in the courtyard," and "the dog has no Buddha-nature"—these are all simultaneous skillful means.
It is like exchanging honeyed fruit for a bitter gourd; or like taking a heavy burden of one hundred and twenty catties and, letting go of it all at once, placing it upon your own shoulders.
You need only know that it is entirely your own precious treasure, to be enjoyed by yourself, and that it will never be exhausted.
A clever person is not deceived by others; they say that everything is nothing but bricks, tiles, and shards, or leftover gruel and spoiled food.

As for the rice, there is no need to laboriously pick it out. The mountains and rivers of the great earth are fundamentally pure; seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are inherently and spontaneously perfected.
Birth and death are like a game; the oceans of lands as numerous as motes of dust and sand do not separate self and other by so much as a hair’s breadth.

Throughout the ten ages of past and present, from beginning to end, there is never a moment of separation from this very thought. It is you yourself who create obstacles; it is you yourself who manufacture difficulties;
it is you yourself who lack self-confidence. *Tut!* What is there to believe? How could you place a head upon a head? How could you attach a handle to a bowl?
If you persist to the death and still do not know where to return, stubbornly wishing to catch the wind and grasp shadows—it will not hinder me as I stand upright.
Raising the backbone of cast iron, throughout all three hundred and sixty joints and eighty-four thousand pores, unify them into a single character "Wu" (無).
With one lift, you raise it up, severing dullness and distraction, and overturning brightness, darkness, form, and emptiness.
At midnight, the golden crow suddenly emerges, illuminating the flowers in the sky and the moon in the water.
The great trichiliocosm is but a bubble on the ocean; all sages and worthies are like lightning flashes. When Yangshan reached this point, his tongue was already as if knotted;
words and phrases were utterly lost. Unable to do otherwise, he reduced himself to fine dust to offer to all the people throughout the great earth. Three thousand.
Outside the village, he covered his nose and slunk away. He has already received thirty blows from this old monk.

You travelers on the road who smell the fragrance and catch the scent—do not mistake poison for *amṛta* (clarified butter). Even if it flows down through your entire body and washes away your very bones, you must still receive that one blow behind the head;
only then will you return to life from death. As for all other half-hearted, indistinct, and hazy understandings...
"Fuzzy-fuzzy! A blind donkey chasing a great crowd, mistaking fish eyes for bright pearls. Here at Yangshan, such things are of no use.
This summer, the three hundred and sixty monks are mostly veterans from various quarters who have finished their formal training;

they carry their staffs and wooden poles with them as they come to this Hall of the *Wan* Character merely to probe the waters. Yet, were the torrents suddenly to pour down and the mountains to topple, they would still be unable to contain the flood."
It does not pass through. Where will you go to meet Xueyan? In the mere interval of a thought, do not be surprised by the thunderclaps and lightning flashes.
Among them, there are many bodhisattvas who have newly resolved to seek the Way; having just entered the monastic community, they do not yet know its depths.
You must strictly avoid allowing poisonous impurities to enter your mind. You must simply be prepared to remain without understanding for a lifetime and apply yourself with earnest, practical effort.
My friend, you must go all the way to the bottom before you can succeed. Do not seek it in the books of the ancients, nor look for it at the lips of the present-day crowd.
Even if you were to learn until you are as flawless as a vessel that holds water without leaking, do not let a person of clear vision take a single glance at you;
it would be like mercury falling to the ground, instantly shattered into a hundred fragments. You must practice authentically; you must awaken authentically. Yama...
"Great King, do not fear much talk. If we discuss the matters of the Gate of the Patriarchal School (Zongmen), it is like the spark struck from flint or a flash of lightning;
south is pointed out as north, the Dipper is changed and the stars are shifted. Its movement is like a swift flame passing through the wind—where could one find its seams or gaps?
Therefore it is said: there is guest and host, essence and function, gathering and releasing, killing and enlivening, reward and..."
Punishment. Sometimes there is full reward and full punishment; sometimes full punishment and full reward; sometimes reward within punishment, and punishment within reward;

sometimes reward is itself punishment, and punishment is itself reward; when both reward and punishment are clearly manifest or not clearly manifest, only then does one perceive reward and punishment.
Sometimes there is full life and full death; sometimes full death and full life; sometimes life...

Killing at the same time, or killing not at the same time; reaching the point where there is a host within a guest, a guest within a host, a guest within a guest, and a host within a host—where guests and hosts intersect and hosts and guests alternate.

In the midst of such casualness, one picks up a single mote of dust, and therein lies such a guest-host relationship, such essence and function, such gathering and releasing, and such life-giving and killing. There is...
Such rewards and punishments—how could they be the fabrications of some elder or fabricated monk who, perceiving only the light of a firefly, thinks it can be deliberated upon?
Nevertheless, in times of great peace there is no need for idle weapons; the unified mountains and rivers are as clear as a mirror.

This is the universal discourse on the incense offering. For those of high caliber who travel to study in various quarters, for those of heroic spirit who seek the Way, every lifting of a foot and every movement of a step must take the precedents of the former masters as their standard.
When Deshan saw Longtan, he blew out the paper candle and reached the very bottom of the source of the Dharma;

upon entering the gate, he struck with a staff, striking through wind and rain. When Linji received three painful blows from Huangbo, his heart and liver were torn out; upon entering the gate, he let out a shout.
Like thunder and like lightning— those others who beckon across the river, those who catch sight of the pagoda pole,
or those at the Ao Shan Inn amidst the sound of the painted horn— are all but travelers on the road, unworthy of mention. You younger and later generations,
failing to distinguish between spring and autumn, unable to tell day from night, are bound together as a single bundle by dullness and distraction, lingering in a state devoid of spirit.
This is the land of death. As I have traveled through various regions seeking the Way, how could I not feel shame and trepidation at not having encountered such a person?

When I sought lodging, there was not a single person who did not say that the matter of birth and death is great and impermanence is swift. Yet, as soon as I stepped across the threshold of the Sangha hall—
Consequently, one does not perceive impermanence, nor does one understand the existence of birth and death;

one merely knows how to join the great throng, eat gruel and rice, defecate and urinate, and simply follow others up and down. Who cares whether you have the Buddha-nature of a dog or the "three pounds of flax"?
"The cypress tree in the courtyard"—upon hearing this, a Buddha appears in the world. Yet it is merely said to be an old bhikṣu from the Western Heaven.
One may truly say that he is entirely unattached, having directly penetrated the ground of great rest, great cessation, and great peace.
Alas, though it seems similar, it is certainly not so. My feet ache and my back hurts; let us sit for a moment in meditation and eat.
A single meal. Both legs feel as if they have been struck by a mallet; it is truly distressing, it is truly a matter of suffering.
Brothers, this very thing is birth-and-death and impermanence. At the time when [death] arrives, this very thing is the state before one's parents were even born.
The original face, manifesting at this very moment—if one can thus comprehend it, without straying for even a single thought-moment, one will personally realize the Tathāgata’s pure Dharmakāya.
Without moving a single speck of dust, one personally enters the Tathāgata’s ocean of jewel-like luminous emptiness;
throughout three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, without departing from the present thought, one pervades worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.
Transcending the present moment, he unfolds hundreds of thousands of immeasurable subtle meanings and expounds hundreds of thousands of immeasurable sublime teachings;
all of these never depart from this very occasion. Can you believe this? If you cannot believe it, then offer this profound mind to the dust-motes and lands.
This is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness: to straighten one's spine of cast iron and hold up the single word "Wu" (No) like Mount Sumeru, resting it upon the crown of one's head.
At such a time, naturally there is no dullness nor distraction; the feet do not ache, nor does the back pain. One remains thus, diligent and focused in every thought-moment.

Thus, without realizing or knowing it, with a single spray upon the ground, one directly beholds the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa bodies of the Buddhas of the three periods of time—the adamantine true essence.
It emits light that shakes the earth, illuminating lands as numerous as motes of dust and sands, all of which become worlds of golden radiance.

The myriad phenomena of the forested universe, the grasses, trees, and groves, all become thrones of precious lotus kings, emitting subtle and wondrous sounds and expounding the subtle and wondrous Dharma.

Universally delivering all sentient beings, they equally attain Buddhahood. To the assembly present here, making no distinction between insiders and outsiders, nor any interval between the near and the distant, nor inquiring as to whether one is of the upper, middle, or lower seat, whether a learner (*śaikṣa*) or one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), or whether they have already transcended the world or have not yet transcended it—all are within this assembly of the King of Mount Sumeru Lamps.
Together with Śākyamuni Tathāgata, they shall receive their prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) over the course of five hundred kalpas.

Afterwards, they simultaneously attained Buddhahood, each presiding over a separate land, each turning the wheel of the Four Noble Truths, and each delivering immeasurable sentient beings—continually delivering those not yet delivered and transforming those not yet transformed, proceeding until the realm of sentient beings was empty, at which point they ceased. This is indeed so;
however, one must turn the light back upon oneself and reflect: who, in truth, is this that attains Buddhahood? Look at the face of that very person!
Even if you have nothing [of substance], you must still examine yourself within your own house:
from morning until evening, have you achieved even a single fragment? Have you attained even a single thread without interruption?
Have you attained even a single thread that does not violate the rules of the monastic community, acting like a true monk? Since this is not the case, you cannot avoid being merely empty.
To consume the offerings of the faithful and to waste one’s time—is this not to betray the original intent of your practice?
Traveling two or three hundred li, or even two or three thousand li, casting yourself away from your hometown, your parents, and your teachers—what kind of matter have you actually accomplished?
Why not exert yourself from within, rouse yourself to diligence, and with courage exceeding courage and vigor exceeding vigor, take up this single word "Mu" (無)?
Like closing one's eyes and leaping over the Yellow River—leaping with all one’s might—there will surely come a time of awakening.
One must simply set a broad deadline while acting with urgency, taking awakening as the standard; one must not...

If you harbor the mind that awaits awakening, you will be obstructed and blocked by that single word "awakening. You would wait until Maitreya descends to be born in this world, yet there would never be a moment of awakening.
(He lets out a shout. What is there to awaken to? Right now, cut off the heads of the Reward-Buddha and the Transformation-Buddha;
there is no second person, no second thought. It is fully realized in every place; it is fully manifest in every place.
The mountains are mountains and the waters are waters; monks are monks and laypeople are laypeople.

Even if one were to split open Mount Taihua and burst through the Yellow River, it would still be nothing more than green water and blue mountains. Idly watching the bamboo joints pass over the wall, they add but a few stalks of new bamboo.

The Imperial Grace is vast and generous; the Buddha-Dharma is reviving as it has never been before. The Way of the Patriarchs lies desolate and the monastic communities are withered and fallen as they have never been at this time.

You, a group of men, from a hundred li, two hundred li, a thousand li, or even two thousand li away, all say you have come to Yangshan Temple to rely upon the great assembly, to draw near to teachers and friends, and to practice Zen and study the Way.
Having investigated and clarified the great matter of birth and death within one's own person, you instead merely follow the crowd and join the ranks;

your karmic consciousness is vast and wandering, contending for self and other, contending for right and wrong, contending for first and last, leaping through the thickets of the monastic community and burying your own true self.
Wasted is the light of time; in vain have I consumed the offerings of the faithful. I have slighted and deceived Heaven and Earth, and been arrogant toward the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

I have failed to exert myself even slightly to shake off my own delusions. Turning back to look at myself, what excellence do I ultimately possess? How shall I practice Zen? How shall I study the Way?
Regarding the great matter of birth and death, how shall I penetrate it? Even if one were to possess a single point of knowledge—

This is merely half-seeing. It is the oral and auditory tradition of erroneous speech, like mistaking a donkey’s saddle bridge for a father’s chin, or pointing to a deer and calling it a horse, or calling a bell a jar.
This is what is meant by "one blind man leading many blind men, pulling each other into a fiery pit.
Seek even one or half of such a person who, beneath the very life-root of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, directly draws a single stroke of the sword. Buddha.
The Patriarch placed his hand on [the disciple’s] crown and took a single step backward; among ten thousand, not one succeeds.

Most people merely gather in their quarters, at their sutra desks, atop the bell towers and drum towers, within the Buddha halls and scripture repositories, or beneath the long corridors, whispering into each other's ears, weighing matters with their conceptual consciousness and providing intellectual commentaries.
They transmit the Buddha-dharma in private, yet fail to realize that these were but the temporary expedients of the ancients.
May you extend your compassion. These stray words and phrases are like insects gnawing through wood, accidentally forming patterns.
If you pursue them with intent or attempt to establish them through substantial reasoning, they will no longer be identical to the whole.

Even if you were to annotate them until they are perfectly clear and explain them until they are thoroughly understood, would you have ever, for even a single moment, severed the cycle of birth and death?
Has it been broken yet? Have you ever opened up the five aggregates and six sense-objects right before your face? Under the gate of Yangshan, we discuss reality and not illusion.
When I was in Jiangzhe, there was a kind of venerable elder living in a great monastery whose mouth was dripping with water;
he stuffed his belly with leftover soup and rancid rice, doing nothing but prying apart and fabricating interpretations of past and present. He would pick up his whisk—
Striking east and knocking west, he unleashes a bellyful of wild fox drool and snot until the ground is strewn with filth, its stench unbearable.
There is a certain kind of person who, failing to distinguish good from evil, seizes upon such foul vapors and calls them the supreme flavor of *amṛta*, treasured by the world.
It is stored within the field of the eight consciousnesses like oil soaking into flour, remaining there forever.

They cannot extricate themselves from their attachments. Habitual tendencies permeate them like incense smoke, causing branches and vines to flourish. Sons are born of fathers, and grandsons are born of sons;

there is none who does not pass this on to one another and cite each other as evidence. Each person claims for themselves that they have realized Zen and realized the Way, yet while they themselves have never attained clarity, they first seek to serve as models for others.
They open rooms to raise koans, accept requests for instruction, and write dharma talks.
They display causes and conditions that fill the paper and exhaust the brush, speaking of mere semblances and tangled vines to deceive the world and blind the later students.

They create the causes for the hells and bind themselves to the fruit of the Avīci hell; even if a thousand Buddhas appear in the world, there will be no way to repent. This is the true reason for traveling on pilgrimage.

For those who cultivate the Way through the true cause and apply themselves with the true cause, you genuine practitioners of the Path must set a broad timeframe while exerting yourselves with urgency,
taking awakening as your standard. If you crave quick results or seek easy entry, you will be enticed by such a faction into the thickets of delusion,
where you will only achieve the views and skills of a wild fox— half-ripe and half-unripe.
Half-yellow, neither distinguishing nor understanding; dim and hazy, vague and indistinct—like a dead man whose soul has not yet dispersed.
Such a person is but a withered sprout and a ruined seed. If you are a man of strength, you must simply resolve that you will never understand in this life.
If it is not resolved in this life, there is still a future life; if it is not resolved in the future life, there is still a subsequent world.
Since vast kalpas past, the ignorance and afflictions of birth and death have shared the same root as heaven and earth;
to undergo a single, complete overturning of this state and surpass the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the Buddhas—how could this not be a difficult matter?

This summer, among the assembly, there are many who are mature and experienced, and few who are not outstanding and talented; half are those who raise their heads and wear horns, and half are those who subdue their claws and hide their fangs.
[The Master] said, "I must resolve the matter clearly regarding the two characters 'birth and death.

For this reason, the heads of the various quarters have exerted themselves to petition at the attendant's quarters, insisting that I, an old monk, burn incense on behalf of the assembly. In my heart, I think: I am seventy years old this year;
one does not rely on physical strength in old age. Let those who become dragons ascend to heaven as they wish; let those who remain snakes follow their own course."
Even a mere blade of grass would not do; how much less so for an old monk like me, who possesses neither Chan nor the Way, neither seeing nor hearing.
Throughout my life, I have not occupied myself with books, nor do I have the capacity for memorization. What could I possibly say? There is only this phrase: "The dog has no Buddha-nature.
I have cast it aside upon a heap of refuse for over forty years. Now, having no choice, I must bring it forth and bestow it upon you all. From—

Teaching them to bite the west and bite the east, chewing crosswise and chewing vertically—suddenly, by a slip of the mouth, they bite through it all. Thereupon, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth;

the myriad phenomena of the forested and the vast; all sink away into total stillness. The entire Great Canon of teachings, its five thousand and forty-eight volumes, and its one thousand seven hundred knots of complications—all melt like ice and crumble like tiles.
Birth and death, as well as coming and going, are no longer obstacles; one is free and autonomous.

As for those who investigate step by step, penetrate step by step, reconcile step by step, and rejoice step by step—there are many such people in the monastic communities; this is not something I know.

Ascending the hall to cite an ancient precedent: The ultimate barrier is as clear as the bright sun; yet if one attempts to deliberate upon it even for a moment, it is as if separated by the Iron Ring Mountains.
When you have reached this point, how can you possibly offer a theoretical explanation? Try to bring it forth. The Elder Śākyamuni was at the assembly on Vulture Peak.
The World-Honored One took up a single branch of a flower, blinked his blue-lotus eyes, and gazed upon the great assembly.
At that time, among the hundred thousand humans and devas, only Kāśyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said:

"I entrust to you the treasury of the true Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, the subtle and wonderful dharma-gate of the formless true mark. You must protect and maintain it, and propagate it so that it never be severed."
I venture to ask the assembly: ultimately, what is called the "Treasury of the True Dharma Eye"?
Since it is the reality-mark (*dharmatā*), how can one explain the principle of formlessness? Furthermore, through what gateway does this subtle and wondrous dharma-door enter?
This single flower held in the hand of the World-Honored One has never been moved; what was entrusted to you that you should now circulate? Do not fail!
It causes [the lineage] to be severed. Furthermore, whom did he instruct to propagate it? Do you know yet? If you do not yet know, listen further.
Yangshan shall explain it for you from the beginning. As for this Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, I dare say that even Śākyamuni himself has not so much as half a cent’s worth of it.
The true mark is markless; precisely because it is markless, the true mark manifests before one. The mountains are green...

"Seeking the mind, it is utterly unobtainable. A single film over the eye causes empty flowers to fall in confusion.

Thus, the Verse of Wondrous Joy says: "Mind is Buddha—do not seek falsely; neither Buddha nor mind—cease seeking elsewhere. Snowflakes fly upon the flames of a red furnace;
a single point of coolness removes all feverish affliction. Now tell me, what are these snowflakes upon the flames of the red furnace?
It flies away. At such a moment as this, what kind of realm is it? Is there still a Buddha to be sought, or a mind to be found?
Listen further to this verse from me, the mountain monk: Speech and silence both forgotten, neither right nor wrong; The sentiments of sage and ordinary exhausted, transcending all mystery.
A swallowtail butterfly is seen deep within the flowers; A dragonfly darts lightly over the water.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Words are uttered yet are not sounds; forms appear yet are not objects. To meet the situation face-to-face, the teaching is fully presented—how could it depend on striking the gavel or raising the whisk?
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth do not obstruct the eye’s vision; the myriad phenomena and the ten thousand images stand upright, their shadows straight. Is there anyone who understands this?"
Let us examine this: While Mazu and Baizhang were walking together, they rolled about in the grass.
Seeing wild ducks fly past, do not follow after sounds or pursue forms. Mazu asked, "What is it?"—something that not even a thousand sages could name.
Baizhang replied, "Wild ducks. He mistook the pivot of the teaching. Mazu asked, "Where have they gone?"—the bright moon and the reeds in the dew.
Anshou: "The hundred-foot pole has flown away. As the evening sun sets in the west and the waters flow eastward, Mazu turns back and seizes Baizhang by the nose.
Indeed, he has fallen into the weeds. Baizhang makes a cry of pain;
Mazu says, "You said it had flown away—this will mislead the men and women of this household. Baizhang attains realization. Those looking on are made to laugh. Mazu.
The ordinary way: whenever one perceives a form, one perceives the mind. The mind is not a mind in itself; it exists because of forms.
Form is the mind; the mind is form. Form is fundamentally not form; the mind is simply no-mind. Being no-mind yet being mind, the total mind is the Buddha.
Being non-form yet being form, the total form is the mind. While Mazu and Baizhang were walking, they saw wild ducks.
The "son" flies away; the great earth, mountains, and rivers are all revealed in their entirety.
Mazu exhausts his compassionate, grandmotherly heart and points directly at Baizhang, asking, "What is this? Baizhang replies, "A wild duck. He has missed it.
Mazu again pressed him with a follow-up question, saying, "Where is it? Baizhang replied, "It flies away; as before, one does not know where it returns.
At this point, Mazu could not help but "injure the salt and vinegar"; he gave Baizhang’s nose a tug.
Baizhang cried out in pain, and Mazu pulled him back, asking, "What is this worth? He then raised his whisk and said:
"You all, do you still see the wild duckling? [The Master] lowered his whisk. "Where is it now?
You people, if you can here sweep away the clouds of delusion and break open the sun of wisdom, you will see that Mazu and Baizhang have failed grievously.
Not only will you see Mazu and Baizhang fail, but you will see Guishan as well."
The Master of the Way saw Huitang discussing this Way. Huitang said, "In the *Analects*, there is the phrase:

'I have nothing hidden from you. Scholar, try to explain it for me. For all his life's skill, Huangbo (Shangu) explained it a thousand ways and ten thousand ways, yet he simply could not accord with Huitang’s meaning.
At this point, Huangbo was at his wits' end and requested further instruction from Huitang. Huitang—
He said, "Scholar, you will understand this of your own accord in time. One day, while they were wandering together in the mountains, they suddenly caught the fragrance of osmanthus blossoms.
Huìtáng then asked Shānyǔ, "What is that fragrance? Shānyǔ replied, "The fragrance of osmanthus blossoms. Huìtáng followed up by saying, "I have nothing hidden from you.
At these words, Shānyǔ attained a sudden and complete realization. Nevertheless, his nostrils had not yet escaped falling into [the trap].
In Huìtáng’s hands—tell me, how far apart is this from Mazu grabbing Baizhang by the nose?
Is Baizhang’s realization the same as or different from the realization of the Wayman Guishan?
If you all can distinguish black from white at this point, I grant that you possess the eye of a student of the Way. Wugou Zhuangyuan saw Miaoxi; with Miaoxi...
Xilun Zhengxin Chengyi asked, "How does one attain knowledge and examine things? Miaoxi said, "The provincial examination winner only knows how to examine things;

he does not know that when things are examined, they are realized. Wugou asked, "What is meant by 'things being realized'? Miaoxi said, "When Emperor Minghuang of the Tang dynasty fled to Shu, he had a portrait executed.
When he was beheaded in Shaanxi, the head fell from the portrait. Upon hearing this account, Wugou became even more bewildered. Thereupon—
While at the latrine, I had an awakening and composed these verses: "Zi Shao [Zhaozhou] said 'the pattern of things' (gewu); Miaoxi [Dongshan Liangjie] said 'things patterned' (wuge).
Originally they are one and the same; two five-hundred-pence coins make one thousand. You people here: to understand "the pattern of things" is easy; to understand "things patterned" is difficult.
Even if you see "things patterned," you cannot escape being pierced through the nostrils by this mountain monk’s whisk.
Set aside the whisk for a moment. Where is the wild duck right now? Listen to this verse: It flew down from above and floated upon the water;
Yet here I ask about its traces. Because it turned its head back, its whereabouts were lost; A single squeeze causes cold sweat to flow over one’s entire body.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Speech is slander; silence is deception. Beyond speech and silence—how can one ultimately approach this? Let us examine it.
When Baizhang went for his second visit to Mazu, Mazu raised up his whisk and inquired after his health, saying, 'May you enjoy ten thousand blessings.
Baizhang said, 'To use this very thing and yet be apart from its use is to create artificial distinctions. Mazu then hung down the whisk."
At the old site, as was the custom, it was still cold during the first month of spring. Mazu asked Baizhang, "After you have opened these two flaps of skin [your mouth], how will you benefit people?
There can be nothing else. Baizhang also held up his whisk. "A true son never uses his father's money," Mazu said.
"The application of this very thing and the departure from this very thing are not different by so much as a hair’s breadth. Baizhang.
He hung his whisk back in its old place; it could not be removed from this spot at all.
Mazu let out a thunderous shout—a truly ugly gesture—whereupon Baizhang attained great enlightenment, to the point that he was deaf for three days. Is this really so?

Often everyone says he attained great enlightenment under the shout, yet they do not realize that "As-wee (A-wei) has no counterfeit, and mercury has no fake. From antiquity to the present day, it has been thus.
The old monks of the world cannot distinguish blue from yellow, nor can they tell beans from wheat; only Xuedou has a slight edge. He said:
"Refined gold from a great furnace should not change its color. Old Fenyang’s verse says:

"By chance, while attending before my teacher, the teacher pointed to something hanging on the corner of the meditation seat. I picked it up and returned to my original position to stand; clearly, a single shout reached [the source]."
The current transmission—applying vermilion and filling in the ink—is not the work of a true master. Zen Master Wenzhen said in verse: "Guest sentiments follow others at every step;
Though there is great majestic light, one cannot see it. Suddenly, a shout deafens both ears; Nata’s eyes open upon Huangbo’s face.
A person of great power turns back within speech and silence. Miaoxi’s verse says: "The horse colt..."

At his feet, the family tradition has been lost; from this day forth, news shall pass through the four seas. To pluck the moon from amidst a mass of fierce flames—to sit alone in majesty upon the Great Hero’s Peak.
There is no lack of principle to be explained, yet if you wish to see Mazu and Baizhang, you are still far away.
Brothers, if you would take up this matter, it is like seeing the corner of a horn from behind a wall and knowing it is an ox; even across a mountain...

Seeing smoke, one immediately knows it is fire. It is like a rushing torrent or a blade’s edge; like a swift flame passing through the wind, by the time you blink your eyes, the sword has long since gone.
At that moment, when Baizhang saw the whisk being raised, he broke it in two.
This is even more laughable. To pointlessly ask whether "this is used" or "separate from this is used" is to have the nose-rope already fallen into the hands of another;

one is then dragged about by him in any direction he pleases. As for his thunderous shout, you instead claim, "At that time I attained great enlightenment, to the point that my ears were deaf for three days. How utterly disheartening! Do you still recognize shame? Mountain.
When the monk arrived here, he saw injustice on the road and sent someone to level it; yet, being few against many, he could not avoid following up with a verse:
A single shout strikes head-on like crashing thunder and lightning; even those who merely hear of it are darkened and their souls tremble.
It appears that it was not merely deafness for three days; it has continued until now, darkening the seas and mountains.

Entering the hall: Within the realm are the sun and moon; beyond measure lies the universe. When raised up, there are a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions; when set down, [all is one].
"Not a speck of dust is established. Try raising it and see. Once, while Baizhang was presiding over the assembly, an old man joined the crowd to listen to the Dharma.
One day, when the assembly had withdrawn, the old man did not leave. Baizhang then asked, "Who is that person before me? The old man replied, "I am no ordinary man.
During the time of the past Kāśyapa Buddha, I once dwelt on this mountain. Because a student asked me about those who engage in great cultivation—"
"A person—do they still fall within cause and effect, or not? The man replied, "They do not fall within cause and effect. [For this] he fell into the body of a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes.
He now requests the Master to provide a turning word on his behalf, so that he may be released from the wild fox's body.

He then asked, "Does a person of great cultivation still fall within cause and effect, or not? Baizhang said, "They are not deluded regarding cause and effect. At these words, the old man was greatly enlightened.
Wu bowed and said, "I have already cast off my wild fox body; I reside in a cave behind the mountain.
I beg that you grant me the rites accorded to deceased monks. The Master ordered the *weina* to announce this to the assembly.

After the meal, the Master personally led the assembly to the cave behind the mountain, where they unearthed the dead wild fox and cremated it according to the Dharma. That evening, he ascended the hall and recounted the preceding events.
[The Master] said, "An ancient once gave a wrong answer to a single turning phrase and fell into the body of a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes.
If one never errs in every turn, what should one do? Baizhang said, "Come closer. Huangbo stepped forward and struck Baizhang with his palm.
Baizhang clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "I thought the beard was red; it turns out there is a red-bearded barbarian too. Situ Tuo cited this previous account.
He asked this of Guishan. Guishan shook the door panels three times.

"If you all can see through to the very bottom at the point where Guishan shook the door panels, you will know that Baizhang before five hundred lifetimes is precisely the wild fox after five hundred lifetimes;
the wild fox after five hundred lifetimes is precisely Baizhang before five hundred lifetimes. You must understand this without falling [into conceptual traps]."
"Is it cause and effect? He pats his left knee and says, "It is here. "Do you wish to understand that cause and effect are not obscured?
He pats his right knee and says, "It is here. Should you still not have realized this, I shall provide a further commentary for all of you.

Whenever Baizhang was in the midst of receiving visitors, there was always an old man who followed the assembly to listen to the Dharma, coldly observing the strengths and weaknesses of others. One day, the assembly...

[The Master] stepped back. The old man did not step back. This was not a kind intention. The Master asked, "Who is that person before me? [The Master] added, "This is like inviting a thief to ruin one's house. The old man said, "He is no ordinary human. [The Master] asked, "Is he perhaps a wild fox? [The old man replied,] "In the time of the past Kāśyapa Buddha, he once dwelt on this mountain. [The Master] said, "Stop talking such nonsense. Because a student asked, "Does a person of great cultivation still fall within the realm of cause and effect? [The Master] said, "He does not. The old man then said, "I have been here for twelve hundred years, yet I have never been able to get rid of this fellow. [The Master] said, "Old fox, you are transformed! [The old man] bowed and departed. The Master then called out, "Old fox! Old fox! You have not yet been transformed! At that moment, the old man turned his head and looked back. The Master struck him with his staff, and he fell to the ground, whereupon he became a stone statue. Later, when the Master was about to pass away, he told the assembly, "When I was at Mount Taishan, I encountered an old man who was not a human being. He said, 'In the time of the past Kāśyapa Buddha, I dwelt on this mountain. I asked him, 'Do those of great cultivation still fall within the realm of cause and effect? He replied, 'They do not. I then asked, 'If they do not fall within it, why did he say he had been here for twelve hundred years? He replied, 'I have been here for twelve hundred years, yet I have never been able to get rid of this fellow. The Master then said, "I have now gotten rid of him. He then passed away. A monk later asked, "What is the meaning of the Master saying, 'I have now gotten rid of him'? The Master said, "He was a wild fox spirit. The monk asked, "How can one tell whether someone is a wild fox or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a wild fox; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a wild fox. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one has attained the Way or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you have attained the Way; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you have not attained the Way. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a Buddha or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a Buddha; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a Buddha. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a patriarch or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a patriarch; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a patriarch. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a sage or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a sage; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a sage. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a worthy or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a worthy; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a worthy. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a teacher or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a teacher; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a teacher. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a master or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a master; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a master. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a person of realization or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a person of realization; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a person of realization. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a man of the Way or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a man of the Way; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a man of the Way. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a true person or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a true person; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a true person. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a saint or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a saint; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a saint. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a noble one or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a noble one; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a noble one. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a realized one or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a realized one; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a realized one. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a master of the Way or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a master of the Way; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a master of the Way. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a person of the ultimate or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a person of the ultimate; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a person of the ultimate. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a person of the highest vehicle or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a person of the highest vehicle; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a person of the highest vehicle. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a person of the Great Vehicle or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a person of the Great Vehicle; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a person of the Great Vehicle. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a person of the Bodhisattva path or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a person of the Bodhisattva path; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a person of the Bodhisattva path. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a person of the Śrāvaka path or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a person of the Śrāvaka path; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a person of the Śrāvaka path. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a person of the Pratyekabuddha path or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a person of the Pratyekabuddha path; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a person of the Pratyekabuddha path. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a person of the worldly path or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a person of the worldly path; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a person of the worldly path. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a person of the transcendental path or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a person of the transcendental path; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a person of the transcendental path. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a person of the ultimate truth or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a person of the ultimate truth; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a person of the ultimate truth. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a person of the provisional truth or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a person of the provisional truth; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a person of the provisional truth. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a person of the middle way or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a person of the middle way; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you are not a person of the middle way. The monk asked, "How can one know whether one is a person of the unconditioned or not? The Master said, "If you speak of the Dharma, you are a person of the unconditioned; if you do not speak of the Dharma, you

"No. [The Master] replied, "It does not fall into cause and effect. [The fox] said, "That was wrong. For five hundred lifetimes, I have fallen into the body of a wild fox. This is now my current lifetime.
I beg the Venerable One to provide a turning phrase on my behalf, so that I may be released from this wild fox body. [The Master asked,] "Why do you speak with human speech?

He then asked, "Does one who practices great cultivation still fall into cause and effect? [The Master] replied, "One does not obscure cause and effect. [The fox] said, "That was wrong. Old [Master Huangbo].
The man attained great enlightenment upon hearing these words. He prostrated and said, "I have shed my wild fox body. I trust half of what you have said;
I reside in a cave behind the mountain. I venture to inform the Master: please grant me the funeral rites accorded to a deceased monk. It is difficult to forget that which one is most familiar with.

The Master ordered the *karmadāna* to announce to the assembly: "After the meal, we shall escort the deceased monk. After the midday meal, the Master personally went to the base of the cliff and pointed out [the location].

"A dead wild fox. [Baizhang] performed the cremation according to the rites. That evening, he ascended the hall and brought up the previous matter. When Baizhang explained that [Nanquan] had failed because his answer was not yet capable of breaking through, Huangbo then asked:
"If an ancient master gave one wrong turn of phrase and fell as a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes, what would he have become had he not made a single mistake?
[Huangbo] replied, "A tiger is originally a tiger. Baizhang said, "Come closer. [Huangbo] thought there must be some other skill or power [in this]. Huangbo—
He stepped forward and gave him a slap—this is "accustomedly stroking the tiger’s whiskers. Baizhang clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "I thought it was a red-bearded barbarian;
there is yet another red-bearded barbarian! Later, when Jiaozhuan struck the ice and hit the frozen surface right down to the bottom, Head Dharma Master Sima raised this as a question for Guishan.
Guishan shook the door panels three times. This was to cover up that wild fox spirit. Later, Master Fachang Yu said: "Although..."
Then the wild fox would have escaped; yet, what could one do about the spittle and froth it vomited? To this day, no one has cleared it away.
When Fachang speaks thus, he only makes things more of a mess. I dare ask you all: why did "not falling into cause and effect" result in falling as a wild fox? It was a mistake.

"Not ignorant of cause and effect. Why did he say, "How could you escape the wild fox? *Wrong*. Even if you can speak so that the point of descent is clear, you have not yet emerged from the den of the wild fox.
*Wrong*. Had I been there at that time, I would first have pulled out Xuefeng’s ancient mirror for him.
He could not be turned by instruction; next, Baizhang brought forth the purple-brown dog to sever its life-force for him.
This too was merely a forced exposition of principle. Have you not seen how Chan Master Zheng of later Baizhang composed this verse?

"The painter paints the hells, Painting out hundreds of thousands of forms. Setting down his brush, he looks from the beginning; Suddenly, my hair stands on end. Do you still feel it at the crown of your head?
Is it heavy? Regarding this koan, those with false interpretations are many, and those who misunderstand it are not few.
Nowadays, there is a certain class of scholastic śramaṇas who call this "the wisdom of differentiation" or "the mind of nirvāṇa. I shall ask you:
when the wind blows and dust rises daily, and when night is dark and day is bright—is this the same as that, or is it different? This mountain monk will now speak according to my own [realization].
I see: it also forms a single verse. Clouds rise over the Southern Mountain; clouds gather over the Northern Mountain. The sound of bells from the upper realm is heard in the lower realm.
Gazing afar at the place where the assembly of monks practices their path, Celestial incense and cassia seeds fall in profusion.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The first signs have already emerged, yet there is no news of their taking form. The Buddhas and Patriarchs are held aloft before their commands have been issued;
the void rubs its forehead in wonder, and the ten thousand phenomena listen in reverence. Tell me, what time is this? Is there such a thing? Try to bring it forth!
Master Huangbo Duanji addressed the assembly, saying: 'All of you here are nothing but fellows who eat dregs of wine. Thus he spoke.
"Wandering monk! Where have you been all this time? Do you still not know that within the Great Tang Empire there are no Chan masters?
At that moment, a monk stepped forward and asked, "But as for those in various quarters who guide disciples and lead assemblies—what of them? Baizhang said, "I do not say there are no Chan masters."
It is simply that there is no teacher. This old fellow has at once crushed his three hundred and sixty joints and eighty-four thousand pores and scattered them all into the laps of you all.

If you can directly accept this right here and now, you may be said to have cut off the heads of both the Reward-Buddha and the Transformation-Buddha without expending the slightest effort. Should you, however, let it slip past you face-to-face—
[The Master] said, "It is past. This mountain monk cannot help but add a point to the arrowhead; let me provide you with another commentary.
All of you here are nothing but fellows who eat dregs of wine. Not only you all, but even the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the three periods of time have been like this.
Traveling on pilgrimage in such a manner—where would there be a 'today' like this? What is the matter of today? Do you know that within the Great Tang Empire..."

"Is there no Chan master? [The Master replied: "There already is windless, rippling wave upon wave. At that time, a monk came forward and said, "As for those in various quarters who guide disciples and lead assemblies—what of them?
[The Master said: "Wrong. The Master said, "I do not say there is no Chan; it is simply that there is no teacher. You blockheads!
All of you, if you could recognize Huangbo before a word is opened and before a tongue moves," [he would be a true master].
The Buddhas and Patriarchs of the three periods of time are under your very feet. If you have not yet realized this, the sword has long since been lost.
Have you not seen how Xuedou’s verse says: "His majestic wind is chilling, yet he does not boast; dwelling serenely within the universe, he settles dragons and snakes.

The Emperor of the Great Tang once lightly provoked him, and thrice he personally encountered his bared claws and fangs. Great or small, Xuedou has exhausted his strength, yet he can only say this much.
This person sits upright, bringing stability to the dragon and serpent within the vast ocean. Yet, at the very end, he cannot avoid finding himself with no way to turn back;

he is instead blown by the wind into a different tune. Elder Dahui’s verse says: "Only by putting on clothes upon one's body can one avoid the cold; merely speaking of food at the mouth will never satisfy hunger.
This 'granny’s Zen' within the Great Tang Empire—I shall now explain it through for you. But even so, there remains a slight discrepancy.
Yangshan imitated [the master’s style] and also composed a verse: "The phrase before the sound surpasses all quarters;
Pointing out heaven and earth as the Great Tang, One sees only the imperial wind forming a single expanse; Who knows where the boundaries of the realm lie?"
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Splitting open Mount Taihua, releasing the Yellow River; blue sky and bright sun, yet wind and waves on level ground.
When one reaches the point where skill is exhausted and strength spent, what has been gained is originally not much.

Linji stayed at Huangbo for three years because the Head Seat instructed him to go to the abbot’s quarters to ask about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma. It was a pitfall that ensnared people—men and women alike. He was struck by Huangbo...

Huangbo struck him twenty blows with his staff and said, "Blind man! This happened three times. With a mind like a silver mountain and an iron wall, he was unable to reach accord and wished to take his leave of Huangbo;
yet, he possessed a measure of the breath of a true man. The Head Seat secretly informed Huangbo, "That young man who asked questions is most extraordinary.
One day he will become a great tree that provides shade for all people under heaven. Later, Linji came.

[Zhaozhou] said, "You may use skillful means to guide them; why such a desperate hurry? Linji took his leave of Huangbo. Huangbo said, "There is no need to go elsewhere; go straight to Dayu. Linji went to Dayu. Dayu asked, "Where have you come from? Linji said, "I have come from Huangbo. Dayu asked, "What were the words and phrases [he spoke]? Linji recounted how he had asked three times and been struck three times. Dayu said, "Huangbo is like an old grandmother; he has exhausted his resources for you, so why do you not go back and ask him, 'When I was wrong, you struck me; when am I not wrong that you will strike me? Linji returned to Huangbo and asked, "Just now, I went to Dayu and told him about my previous experience. He said, 'Huangbo is like an old grandmother; he has exhausted his resources for you; why do you not go back and ask him, "When I was wrong, you struck me; when am I not wrong that you will strike me? Huangbo said, "If you go again, I shall beat you even more severely than before. Linji immediately gave a shout and left. As soon as he reached the mountain gate, he had a great realization. He returned to Huangbo and said, "I have attained it! Huangbo said, "What did you attain? Linji said, "From this day forward, I shall never again doubt the Buddhas or patriarchs. Huangbo said, "You have finally let me down. Linji then bowed and departed. That night, he went to the abbot's quarters and knocked on the door. The attendant inside asked, "Who is it? Linji said, "It is a monk who has just arrived from the west. The attendant said, "The Master is resting; wait until morning. Linji said, "If you tell him it is a monk who has just arrived from the west, I will give you thirty blows of the staff. The attendant went in and told the Master. When these are applied and transformed, they become Zhaozhou’s "Cypress Tree," Yunmen’s "Dry Dung," Deshan’s "Staff," and Linji’s "Shout.
When rolled up, they form the "Mysterious Barrier" and the "Golden Lock"; when unfolded, they manifest as ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences. To speak in Confucian terms...

They speak of it as the Imperial Ultimate (Huangji), as the Mean (Zhongyong), and as the Great Learning (Daxue). When these are synthesized and brought back to their source, they are none other than the "loyalty and reciprocity" of the Master Kong and the "magnanimous qi" of Mencius;
they are the very essence of Yan Hui’s “simplicity” and Zengzi’s “attentiveness,” manifested as the Odes and Documents, and as Ritual and Music.
They are arranged into the Three Bonds and the Five Constant Virtues. Viewed from this perspective, the locus of the Way in both Confucianism and Buddhism is certainly one and the same;
it is only because their transformative influences differ that their regulations are not identical. Why is this?

It is because the teaching of Buddhism takes compassion and forbearance as its transformation and precepts and meditative concentration as its regulation. Consequently, when people encounter it, they may observe it at leisure, yet even when approaching it closely...
The teachings of the *Yijing* and the Confucians take sincerity and illumination as their transformation and punishment and retribution as their regulation.
Therefore, people revere and honor them; they look up to them with awe. When one looks up with awe, fear arises; when something is near and easy, negligence arises.

Now, if people truly say, "I am arrogant," then those refined gentlemen who have transcended the world and severed themselves from the dust of the mundane—those pure and cool souls—would sweep [away such negligence].
With my tracks extinguished and my traces vanished, I am content to transform together with the passing flow of time; what trace of worldly phenomena could there possibly be? Therefore it is said:
if one does not rely on the external protection and support of kings and ministers, one may fail to establish oneself.

If one truly fails to establish oneself, then those multitudes who merely borrow forms and attire to mingle within the Dharma-gate will overflow its precincts; how then could they know that within my breast and sleeves there is indeed something firm and real?
This is indeed the Way that may be revered and esteemed, that may be looked up to, and that may be both feared and dreaded.
I venture to say that the most essential point of the Buddha-dharma is rooted in the illumination of the mind. To desire the mind to be thoroughly illuminated, one must value the cessation of views.

If views do not cease, then the heterodox and the orthodox will intermingle; if the mind is not illuminated, then the true and the deluded will race against one another. If [views] are truly ceased...
It is clear: both truth and falsehood are empty; neither the heterodox nor the orthodox can be established.

Directly beneath, one is simply blunt and unrefined, broad and uncouth—like an old peasant from a village of three households, with not a hair’s breadth of intellectual views to ensnare the mind, and not a hair’s breadth of sound or form to cloud the ears and eyes.
Even when reaching such a state, one remains as ever topsy-turvy, whether facing adversity or favor.
Moving freely in all directions—left and right—being nowhere yet not being anywhere: only then can it be said that the mind is enlightened and the breath has ceased.
Delusion and depravity cannot interfere; correctness and rectitude need no longer be looked toward. Yet one must further shift the pivot of the upward gate and overturn everything at once.

All these flow forth from within this Great Perfect Enlightenment; there is not even a hair’s breadth of anything that comes from without.

Thereafter, whether it be the Buddha or the mind, seeing or cessation, the heterodox or the orthodox, the real or the delusory—there is no need for further differentiation, as they are all clearly discerned within the bright mirror.
I, Jingxi, have humbly observed that the Way of the Sage and the Way of the Tathāgata are one and the same Way; they have never been two.
The Way of the Sage consists in following one’s nature, while the Way of the Tathāgata consists in realizing one’s nature. By realizing one’s nature, one can then clarify the mind.

One can thereby attain Buddhahood; one can thereby deliver sentient beings. By following one's nature (*xing*), one can rectify the mind, cultivate the person, govern the state, and bring peace to all under heaven. Although "following" and "seeing" differ, their nature is the same.
It is not only that the Sage and the Tathāgata share this same single nature; from Zengzi, Zisi, and Mencius down to recent times, it has been so as well.
In this world, there were Yi Lu, Hei-an, Shui-xin, and Yun-men; as well as Jing-xi, An-fu, Du-yun, and Shi-lang.
Their authentic lineage has continued in an unbroken thread, and those who have followed in succession have reached the realm of the Sage; they all shared this same nature.
From the thirty-five patriarchs of India and China down to De-shan, Lin-ji, and more recently, Miao-xi and Ying-an—whether they had passed away or remained in the world—[all realized this].
Occasionally there have been practitioners who emerged to propagate the secret mysteries of the Buddhas and Patriarchs that had not been transmitted;
beyond words and phrases, they were likewise of this same nature. Since this nature is the same, this Way is also the same.

Since this Way is the same, then the books of the hundred schools and various Confucian scholars and the texts of the five thousand scrolls of the Great Canon are one and the same tongue. Therefore, the Sage—
[The Master] said: "My Way is one that runs through all things. The Tathāgata also said: "In the worlds of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma.
Now, this Dharma of the Single Vehicle and the Way that runs through all things are this very nature; this nature is this very Dharma.
This Dharma is this very Path. It is the Path; it is the Dharma; it is the Nature (*dharmatā*). Their names differ, but their substance is one.
As for its substance: Heaven encompasses all without exterior; it enters the finest details of autumn hair. One may welcome it and not see it; one may cast it aside and it is ever-present.
Heaven and earth rely upon it to stand; the sun and moon rely upon it to shine; the sages rely upon it to establish their teachings; and the Tathāgata relies upon it.

This is what is manifested; it is what the Confucians call the "Supreme Ultimate" (Huangji), the "Ultimateless" (Wuji), and the "Great Ultimate" (Taiji), and what the Buddhists call the "Original Radiance," the "Original Face," and the "Parents from Whom One Is Born.

To bring peace to great households and to grant leniency to the common people—this is truly said to be the fulfillment of the Way of rectifying the mind and sincerity. He has practiced and exerted himself in this;

It fell to the ground in despondency. Even now, I have not yet fully realized this mind; I have come here to form an alliance for this Way.

Indeed, this original countenance and the natural radiance of the fundamental ground—akin to the Great Ultimate (Dàjí) and the August Ultimate (Huángjí)—are so vast and so expansive that they cannot be described or conceptualized.
Therefore, its expressions are for the most part broad and open, while its underlying principles are for the most part profound and hidden. Thus...

Through its profound and hidden depths, one perceives its wondrousness; as bright as the light of day, through its vast openness, one perceives its subtlest details, as close as the hairs on one's eyebrows and eyelashes.
There is nothing of this principle’s profundity or its expansive clarity that does not manifest within this mind;
it is never concealed. Therefore, the Sage said: "Do you think I have anything hidden? I have nothing hidden."
Thus it is. The Tathāgata has also said: "Dharma after dharma is not concealed; from antiquity to the present, it is ever manifest.
Yet this meaning, though most near and most simple, cannot be reached by the worldly intelligence or sharp wit.
It requires that one cast off all emotional dust and intellectual pathways until, within the space of an inch in one's breast, it is as vast and open as the great void. Then, this—
The meaning is perfectly clear. Furthermore, one immediately knows that the myriad phenomena of the universe—the insects, plants, and trees—are this very meaning;
joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure, as well as every movement of bending, turning, bowing, and rising, are this very meaning.

Once this meaning is clarified, then the books of the hundred schools and various Confucian scholars, and the teachings of the five thousand scrolls of the Great Canon, do not equal even a single character [of it]. Formerly, Prime Minister Li Ao saw...
