Jingxi’s Letter to Administrative Commissioner Wu of Wudu:

I have observed that the Way of the Śākya clan takes the three trainings of precepts, concentration, and wisdom as its core. As for the precepts, they are the discipline by which the mind is maintained.
Concentration (samādhi) stills the mind so that it may reflect; wisdom (prajñā) brings intelligence so that the mind may be enlightened.

If one possesses wisdom but lacks concentration and ethical discipline (śīla), then every thought-moment will remain in negligence; such a person merely engages in empty discourse and cannot sever saṃsāra or escape birth and death.

If one possesses concentration but lacks ethical discipline and wisdom, then every thought-moment will remain in vacuous stillness; such a person merely stagnates in inert emptiness and cannot proclaim the Great Teaching.
Among sentient beings, those who possess precepts but lack concentration and wisdom will, moment by moment, remain caught in grasping;

they merely constrain themselves to formal rules yet are unable to unify right and wrong or equalize self and others. However, wisdom is itself concentration, and concentration is itself precepts. Precepts can give rise to concentration, and concentration gives rise to wisdom.
As for wisdom, concentration, and precepts, they are rooted in the one mind. This mind is fundamentally non-existent; such are the precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
Furthermore, from what could it be obtained? Thus, though non-existent, it exists; as vast as the great void, it pervades the entire *trichiliocosm* of sand-grain worlds.
The grasses, trees, and forests, the birds, beasts, humans, and livestock, as well as the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), are all in total this very mind.

When the mind does not give rise [to delusion], it is precept (*śīla*); when the mind does not move, it is concentration (*samādhi*); when the mind is not obscured, it is wisdom (*prajñā*). Precept, concentration, and wisdom are simply this mind.
It is the fundamental endowment of all beings; from the very beginning, it does not depend upon cultivation to be attained.
At times it is not manifest, being as subtle as the tip of a hair, yet it corresponds to all *tathatā*, *prajñā*, *bodhi*, and *vimukti*, as well as the eighty-four thousand practices and vows.

In total, none of these are apart from this mind. The mind is not the precepts, yet it spontaneously ceases [evil]; the mind is not meditative concentration, yet it spontaneously rests; the mind is not wisdom, yet it spontaneously penetrates.
Precepts, concentration, and wisdom, together with this mind, are all devoid of form or characteristics. Although one practices them from time to time, there is nothing to be attained.
In the state of non-attainment, there is nothing that cannot be attained; thus, one attains that which is fundamentally unattainable. This attainment of non-attainment is true attainment.
As for this attainment, it is vast and expansive yet not external; it is tranquil and solitary yet not internal. One looks for it as if it were before one, and suddenly—
It lies behind; it cannot be grasped. It is neither taken up nor discarded; it cannot be named and cannot be described.

This is the singular, extraordinary cause and condition through which hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and patriarchs have transmitted vessel to vessel and reflected mirror upon mirror—what is called the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvana.
For this reason, the Great Master Bodhidharma came from the kingdom of Western India.
When he first met Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, the Emperor asked, "Among the holy truths (*āryasatya*), which is the foremost?
Bodhidharma replied, "Vast emptiness; there is no sage. He was asked again, "Who is it that stands before me? He replied, "I do not know.

This was Bodhidharma directly pointing out this very mind to Emperor Wu, using words to indicate the wordless. The Emperor did not attain resonance with this, so Bodhidharma subsequently broke his reed staff.
He crossed the river and went directly to the foot of Mount Shaoshi, where he sat facing a wall, motionless and steadfast.

This was yet another instance of pointing directly to the mind for all sentient beings throughout the great earth, using wordlessness to manifest that which has words. Nine years of seasons passed, yet no one grasped his intent.
Only Master Daokai Shenguang severed an arm, performed three prostrations, and stood with palms joined in silence.
To shoulder the entire burden before form and name have even emerged—this is what is called the coming of Dharma from the West.

Not establishing written words, pointing directly at the human mind, seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood. From this point on, the poison flowed eastward; people received the echoes and inherited the void.

Among them, Huairang’s engagement with disciples was swift and incisive, like a thunderclap or a flash of lightning. His branches and streams spread in all four directions, distributed like stars and arranged like chess pieces, flowing on and on without end.

For five, seven, or eight hundred years, [the Dharma] has gradually reached the point of extinction and ceased to be heard.

Even in our own region of Zhejiang, a land of great prosperity, the monasteries therein are for the most part defiled and impure; one seeks in vain for those who deeply understand this Way and tread each step with solid reality—such have not been found.
Even those who truly possess this Way and move forward step by step at all times are rare. Since the Way is thus not clearly understood, furthermore...
This is not to be believed. If one desires that the teaching of our Buddha and Patriarchs be revived here, can it possibly be achieved?
For those practitioners who possess even a slight aspiration for study and the dissemination of the Dharma, how could they not feel deep anguish and heave great sighs upon encountering this?
Such as I am, having shaved my head since childhood, I have traveled far and wide out of firm faith in this Way.

Day followed night, and night reached dawn; it was my absolute resolve to dissect this mindfulness and shatter this mind in order to see [the truth].

The original face prior to the birth of one's parents—suddenly, on a certain day, at a place where effort cannot reach, where this thought and this mind have not yet sprouted, it melts away like ice dissolving;
suddenly and completely revealed, it is like the bright moon in the vast void, shining alone in the midnight sky.
At that moment, looking upward, no Buddhas are seen; looking downward, no sentient beings are seen.

Within, one does not perceive a self; without, one does not perceive mountains or rivers. Sublime and majestic, brilliant and radiant, there is only pure clarity—without dependence and without desire.
This is the realm of great liberation, which is what was previously called "the attainment of non-attainment";
this is true attainment. Furthermore, even precept, concentration, and wisdom have no place to be contained. Since precept, concentration, and wisdom have no place...
If you can accept and embrace them, then all opposition and compliance, right and wrong, good and evil, long and short—like clouds in the vast void—what do they have to do with me?

I respectfully consider that you, Excellency the Commissioner, are a national historian and a treasure of literary culture; you are a Vice Minister of the Ministry of War and a true successor to the orthodox lineage of the Way and its Learning, following the tradition of Jingxi Zhiyi.

He has attained the orthodox transmission of Yi, Zhou, Kong, and Meng. Integrous, lucid, benevolent, and compassionate, he is truly a peerless figure in his time for instructing scholars and nourishing the people.
What profound good fortune have I possessed in my past lives that I have encountered such a person at this moment? This is indeed a once-in-a-thousand-year opportunity.
His honorable promotion to Longxing Temple and his transfer to Daolin Temple reflect an extraordinary degree of favor, far exceeding what I had dared to hope for. [The four wonders.]
In the hall, I was fortunate enough to hear his discourse on the Infinite (Wuji). The Vice Minister stated that "the Infinite" refers to this very principle, which is without limit or end.
He further remarked that the teachings of Confucius and Mencius are thus, the teachings of the Yi and Luo schools are thus, and the teachings of Hui-an and Xiang-shan are likewise thus;
it is by perceiving this principle that one sees it to be without limit or end. However, as for this principle...

Since the Ultimate is without limit, phenomena are likewise without limit. Phenomena originally have no names; they are obtained through principle. Principle originally has no form; it is manifested through phenomena.

Beginning from the opening of heaven and the cleaving of earth, down to the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, and throughout the successive generations of rulers and ministers—with their alternating periods of order and chaos, and their cycles of rise and fall—this is the infinity of phenomena. Phenomena do not establish themselves; they exist because of principle.
This reveals that principle is precisely the mind. Heaven, earth, and the myriad things are born within my mind; order, chaos, prosperity, and decline flow forth from this very heart.
Therefore it is said: "Matters originally have no names; they are obtained through principle. The mind is principle itself.
Thus, through the succession of the four seasons and the myriad things, as well as through order, chaos, prosperity, and decline, one perceives this mind. This is the inexhaustibility of principle.
Therefore it is said: Principle is fundamentally formless, yet it manifests through phenomena. Phenomena are principle; principle is phenomena.
When phenomena and principle are fused, this is the ultimate. As for this ultimate, it is vast and expansive, profound and mysterious;
it cannot be exhausted and cannot be depleted—this is the Infinite (Wuji). The ultimate of the Infinite is the Great Ultimate (Taiji). The Great Ultimate is the Center.

Furthermore, "Centrality" (*zhong*) refers to heaven, earth, and the myriad things. It is the ultimate principle of pure vacuity that exists prior to the manifestation of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure.
This principle of pure vacuity contains and harbors heaven, earth, the myriad things, and the emotions of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure;
this is what is called Centrality. As for this Centrality, it is as perfectly round as the Great Void—neither deficient nor redundant—and it can level out all heights.

It is below, yet it does not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence. This is precisely what our Buddha calls the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye (*saddharmapuṇḍarīka-kośa*), what Mencius calls the "Vast and Unfettered Qi" (*haoran zhi qi*), and what Confucius calls the "Way of the Single Thread" (*yiguan zhi dao*).
Through this convergence, although the schools of Confucianism and Buddhism differ in their gateways, that which constitutes the Way is but one.

"Associate with the upright, associate with the trustworthy, associate with the learned"—this is the bequeathed instruction of the sages. To be upright is to open one's heart and manifest sincerity; to be trustworthy...

It was also said in antiquity: "In choosing friends, one must seek those superior to oneself; those who resemble me are better off having none. Such is the way of taking friends.

You have certainly humbled yourself by adopting the title "Friend of the Mountain" (*Yǒushān*). Is this not where the essence of culture resides? Piercing the heavens and uprooting the earth yet remaining independent—this is the integrity of the mountain.
When the wind comes, the trees move; when the leaves fall, one knows autumn. This is the integrity of the mountain. When the bell tolls, the valley responds;
when the monkeys cry and the cranes call, is this not the mountain’s great learning? Now, that the Master takes the mountain as his companion is due to these three virtues.
Indeed, virtue can benefit us. For the mountain is both still and concentrated; within this stillness and concentration, precepts and wisdom arise spontaneously.

It is fitting. That I have now taken the mountain as my companion—is this not for no small reason? May he continue to dwell in peace amidst the crags and cliffs, and may his spiritual influence benefit all beings. The Chan practitioner Muweng Xu Jingxing, though his years in the monastic order are few, possesses an exceptionally profound aspiration. His spirit is as serene as autumn water, and his temperament is as resilient as morning frost.
Having sought the Way from the elder Xueyan, he seems on the verge of attaining realization; yet he has further inquired about the matter of a dharma name. For now—
He then inscribed the two characters "Wu-weng" (No Elder) as a plaque. This too is one method for encouraging progress.

If one can penetrate the source beneath the character "wu," then practice will be perfected without training, and purity will be clear without being sought. What hindrance could there be in being called an "elder" while still young?
The Master further showed him a verse, which said: "The myriad dharmas, layer upon layer, are gathered in a single word; When picked up, they are instantly present."
The tip of the nose; a mass of white hair seen in the mirror. Face-to-face, when has there ever been Zhaozhou?
Clouds and mountains unfold as white clouds linger; green mountains are majestic, the radiant wind is vast, and the clear moon shines brightly. It is like the vision of Sudhana.
"O youth, when you and the Bhikṣu Meghashiri met upon a separate peak, there was neither person nor environment, neither phenomenon nor principle;
neither present nor past—not even a speck of dust intervened, nor did a single hair’s breadth shift.

When the Master addressed himself as 'Eternal Virtue' (Yongde) and styled himself 'Cloud Mountain' (Yunshan), he suddenly rose up and said: 'I am originally nameless; it is only by borrowing the name "Eternal Virtue"..."
He said, "I originally have no title; I have merely borrowed 'Cloud Mountain' as my own name. Would you, Master, be willing to grant me a word as a seal of certification? [The Master] replied, "Yes.
"When learning reaches the state of non-existence, all phenomena are emptied; not even a single speck of dust can be grasped.
This is precisely what Sudhana personally witnessed from the venerable De-yun during those seven days. How could it ever be reached through mere temporary hearing or seeing?"
For this reason, the Master names himself Yongde (Eternal Virtue). Since his virtue is eternal, his Way is likewise eternal.
The Master’s title, Yunshan (Cloud Mountain), is indeed a reality and not a mere fiction. Therefore, I have written this verse to commemorate him: Casting one's gaze without artifice, looking thus:
Supporting heaven and uprooting earth, all is dark and vast. Who would have known that for seven days we shall not meet? It lies right here upon the brow.
In a single inch of space:
A Preface by Jingshan (with verse).

When the myriad conditions do not intrude, the myriad dharmas are naturally at rest; this is the meaning of stillness (*śānti*). Stillness leads to concentration (*samādhi*); concentration leads to peace. What [is attained] therein...
It means being as stable as Mount Tai, such that even ten thousand affairs cannot disturb him. Yet, stillness must be followed by movement; movement must result in action;

and action must result in speech. It is from this that the two characters "Mountain" (Shan) and "Stillness" (Jing) were obtained, and it is from this that he was given the title "Pujie" (Universally Quiescent).
Xueyan’s single verse was also formed on this account. The verse says: "A single track, nothing remains; ten thousand pipes are hushed.
The mountain peaks and moonlight are both profoundly deep. Who would have known that there is still this child making a clamor? The dragon roars within the withered tree of frost."
Preface to *Autumn River* (with verse):

"Autumn River" is the self-appellation of the venerable master Zhìyuè. When the cool autumn moon is bright and the empty river’s waves are calm, all above and below are of one color, and both inside and out are transparently clear.
Mind, Buddha, Chan, the Way, name, and appellation—search for even one [of these] and you shall find none.

The slightest trace of form is utterly unattainable; is this not the realm of vision of the Superior Man? If it were merely this, it would still be a matter belonging to the side of afflictions and obstacles.
To show this briefly, I offer this verse: The shimmering silver river flows through the jade palace, Pure as white silk, with cool light floating.
The Old Barbarian could not step upon it with his single reed-raft; It fell scattered at the head of the broken embankment in the autumn wind.
Preface to Zhongshan (with Inscription) Within the realm of heaven and earth, amidst the expanse of the universe, there is a single treasure hidden within the mountain of form.
Since the ancients have already presented it face-to-face, what is there to hide? The Dharma-treasury keeper Dao takes "Zhongshan" as his own name; since the mountain has been established...
Within the center, there is the external; the internal and external support one another, and thus the secret may be seen. The old master Xueyan inscribed this verse:
"Not leaning" is called the center; "standing firm" is called the mountain. White clouds surround it on all four sides; the bright moon shines within its single chamber.
Sitting alone with the heavenly mind, maintaining right mindfulness, he penetrates straight through Mount Sumeru as if it were but a trivial matter.

Tianquan Shuo succeeded Chu Shi as an attendant. He styled himself Tianquan and requested an explanation from the elder Xueyan, saying: "What is the meaning of this? It is like a piece of wood that has rotted away and is not gathered;
it spans thousands of millions of kalpas without being subject to the passage of spring and autumn, and it has never been touched by the axe of carving or engraving."
The calamity of being hewn down is that it maims my body; the burden of being relied upon as a ridgepole or beam is that it weighs upon my shoulders.
Embracing mist and clouds for my own delight, I sleep idly amidst moss and lichen. Thus, with steady and expectant composure—this is what is called "the perfection of Heaven.
I replied, "No. 'The perfection of Heaven' means perfecting one's Heaven; each person must perfect that which has been bestowed upon them."
In the Way of Heaven, that which is sharp is not dull; the foolish are not wise; the straight are not crooked; and the brittle are not firm. Furthermore, that which is loved is expansive;
the solitary is focused; the grasping is square; and the revolving is round. Others may say it is otherwise, but I say it is so.
Thereupon, he uttered a verse to praise his renown, extol his virtue, and manifest his perfection. His perfection is that of Heaven:
vast, immeasurable, and boundless; it covers the three thousandfold world-systems and the great chiliocosm, leaving no trace of deficiency or partiality.
Its movement should be as circular as that of the sun.
Inscription for One Brook. Inscription.
The mountain stream is so clear it may serve as a mirror; ten thousand currents share a single source. The unsurpassed, wondrous Way can be transmitted only through the mind.
"Daoqing" (Way-Purity) was his name, and a single stream was named after him. As for this composer of the inscription, who is Xueyan?
Inscription on the Iron Boat (Ji):

This great vessel of today is not of the same category as wooden craft. It opens the bellows of heaven and earth and serves as the mold for the Nine Provinces; it kindles the celestial fire of one's inherent nature.
The stone melts and the gold flows; form and name are not yet fully established. The journey has already reached its completion; no oars or rudders are added.
It is both heavy and light, broadly ferrying across the four seas, leaving one’s departure or stay to chance. Under a single sail of bright moonlight, ten thousand miles of clear autumn.
A verse in praise of the Dharma Master De Fuzang:
Like a small sleeping tiger beyond the clouds, his fur is golden-spotted and his majesty extends for a hundred paces; the true eye upon the crown of his head blazes like the dry sky.
*Kūn*: Ordinarily, wind and rain may arise at any time. Leaving home at dawn, where will you go? Visit your kin and old friends within the city of Hengyang;
mark the time and return immediately. With a single clap of thunder, he finished this final verse.
Seeing Master Guang off to the Rear Hall (with Preface):
The Head Seat Miaoguang has been my companion for two years, yet it has felt as though it were but a single day.

He was so diligent in his pursuit of the Way that he was unaware how easily time slips away. Suddenly, he requested a verse to part from him; thus, I have penned this to see him off. The spring wind is harsh.
The spring wind is cruel; in a single night, it has blown all the plum blossoms away. A person comes to speak of parting, about to travel to Wu;

he treads upon the very corner of the heavens in the southeast. The spring wind is cruel. The spring wind is cruel. From eight thousand li away, he gazes toward Western Sichuan; everything that came before was but error.
Beyond the golden robe of the Venerable Master Songzheng, what else is transmitted? You should topple the gate-pillar before the Gate of Response.

This phrase that upholds the Dharma through all antiquity and all time—look with the eyes of realization before the sound! This very thing is the robe and bowl of the patch-robed monk; you have now attained the correct [Dharma].

The Essential Purpose: Entrusted to Ji Yun, this is a separate transmission in a single fascicle. Among those of exceptional talent, you were first among the few; yet suddenly you have requested leave to return to Qingjiang.

Before the window, the plum blossoms of early spring are gradually fragrant. A branch extends horizontally beyond the azure mist; the sound of the spring water sprays like snow as the mountain stream flows with incense-like fragrance.
When the primordial chaos has been resolved for the venerable monk Huìhóng, the brilliant sun appears spontaneously; heaven and earth open in clarity.

"The mind itself is Buddha"—within the ocean of lands as numerous as motes of dust, radiance shines everywhere. Not even a single hair’s breadth can obscure it; you must, however, overturn it directly and immediately—do not hesitate.
What you grasp through knowledge and views is merely this ordinary state; there is nothing further mysterious, wondrous, or extraordinary.

Were this the case under the gate of a true monk, one could not avoid receiving thirty blows of the heavy staff. For now, I shall grant you four rattan canes; go as you please to the east, west, south, or north.
Turning my head toward Mount Jiyun, a verdant peak looms abruptly before me. I bid farewell to Chan Master Ningshang, whose spiritual affinity with the Buddhas and Patriarchs is profound;
his person is naturally healthy and at peace, his conduct is earnest and his speech sparing. His reputation is fragrant and his virtue is sweet, untainted by even a speck of dust.

A thousand li ahead lies the journey; the waters of Fanyang are vast and surging, the clouds atop Jiyun Peak are deep green. Steadily rowing a small boat with short oars, the western wind leaves the waves calm.
— By the Monk Shaolong.
Practice is inherited through virtue; the Way flourishes with the times. Worldly frivolity lies elsewhere, while integrity and steadfastness reside within oneself.

Though their clothing is simple, their conduct remains identical; their Way, virtue, speech, and action are truly luminous. In their words and silences, their movements and stillnesses, they shine like the sun and moon;

in their every turn and bow, they give rise to the spring breeze. This eminent monk spent the summer at Jiyun Peak; suddenly, his desire to return to the Xiang River grew intense. Before the courtyard—
The well-trees and paulownias rustle and sway; with bare shoulders, he carries a lean staff.
The Venerable Zhenhui considers himself the Tathāgata, yet his wisdom, precepts, and samādhi—though these words may be true, this intention has not yet been realized. It is just like the Xiang River.
Half of both [sides] are clear; the mountain face does not open its clouds, which hang thick and heavy. One day ascending to heaven, the four seas are bright;
with the staff-tip turned upward, the head becomes light. Without shifting a single step, he arrives at Tancheng; meeting him, they speak clearly of their future paths.
Master Bonrai has never come from the beginning, nor does he go anywhere. For one hundred and twenty days he remained thus.
Last night, the western wind suddenly shifted its course, and osmanthus trees blossomed by the railing. Gathering his travel bag and folding his sitting mat, he came from Donghu at Jiyun.
In the interval of departure, the cold news from the tips of the twin cassia branches is just like the fragrance of the lotus.
Upon hearing the report, the venerable monk Qingyi attained realization;
with one thing known, all matters are concluded. What joy has filled his life today! The single transmission of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is a mind without duality.
Life and death are utterly transparent; the four walls are empty. Hastily hearing the news of his passing, he returns home, unimpeded in his solitary journey and independent stance.
The myriad peaks are layered in chaotic green; the distant waters shimmer with vacant azure. Within the vastness of heaven and earth, what limit is there to coming and going?
The brilliance of spring turns of its own accord, leaving no trace behind.

Throughout the twelve periods of the day, by whose power do you receive grace? Whether bowing, looking up, turning, or walking, there is no need to seek it elsewhere. When putting on clothes or eating a meal, once it is done, it is simply done.
When opening one's eyes, it is as bright as day—who does not know this? This is the single eye of the śramaṇas of the great earth. One zhang.
The six golden bodies are but a single blade of grass.

The superior man whose will is fulfilled sets his mind on humility and does not allow himself to be self-satisfied. Do not use your own length to stride over the shortness of others. It is because the ocean has limits that even heaven—
Deafness. No one possesses virtue who relies on their keen hearing. Have you not seen how the waters dry up and the mountains wither when things grow emaciated?
When spring arrives and the breeze is mild, butterflies and bees emerge. If you wish to stand firm amidst the thicket, you must study to fulfill your aspirations.

The spiritual and wondrous mechanism of Master Zuji is such that even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot know it. To be too hasty is to miss it; to be too slow is inappropriate. The spirit resides within oneself;
the wonder lies in daily life. Whether eating a meal or putting on clothes, whether still or moving—when both movement and stillness are forgotten, the waves cease and the mountain stands tall.
The Venerable Yuánjué is wondrously enlightened, pure, and clear. Originally there is nothing to be awakened to, like the Poyang Lake when its autumn waves do not stir;

it is also like Mount Kuānglú, where clouds level the moonlit ravines. With a bamboo hat atop his head, he wanders idly amidst the western wind; at the tip of his staff, all is empty and desolate. Smash it!
The shell of the numinous tortoise: the Venerable Zhizhong’s wisdom is far-reaching;
his spiritual mechanism turns spontaneously, like a pearl rolling on a platter, resembling a garden of ten thousand flowers whose blooming and falling do not depend [on external conditions].
In the Spring and Autumn [Annals], movement and stillness are unhindered by coming or going. Clouds drift on, waters flow on; beyond the heavens, the moon is like a hook.
Xuefeng rolls out three wooden balls.

The Venerable Kewen has set a fixed term for his realization; his meritorious practice is now complete. From Xiangnan to Tanbei, the moon shines throughout the month; deep within the Five Peaks, the myriad phenomena are brilliantly clear.
There is no need to pat each other on the back upon meeting—strike him three times hard under the ribs! He is truly one who seizes the wind and seizes the madness.

Awakening to the primordial state of the Supreme Person is the beginning of spiritual awakening. Vast and empty like the great void, clouds settle upon mountain peaks and the sea moon shines upon coral reefs. No description can equal it;
no painting can equal it; no verse can equal it. This single segment of numinous light is peerless through all antiquity and the present. It is originally the bridgehead to Tuṣita Heaven.
The luminous pearl in the night within the Triple Treasury:
that which can be spoken of as the Way is not the eternal Way; that which can be named is not the eternal name. Since names are not eternal, they are like the resonance within a vessel.
The Way is not constant; it is like the light of the sun, like the resonance within a vessel.
Just as the light of the sun shines without limit, so too can one be called a possessor of the Way only when they do not merely cultivate themselves alone, but extend their virtue to all nations.

The Way follows the superior person; one simply follows the Way. One takes the mind alone as the fundamental principle. Emptiness is precisely form; form is precisely emptiness. Dreams and illusions are clearly understood;
coming and going are hurried and fleeting. Like the moon in water, like the wind in the trees—contemplating in this manner, there is no obstruction and nothing that does not penetrate.
Master Liaoming has thoroughly understood and clearly realized. His solitary radiance is bright and pure; the night is long and the moon is cold, yet when the clouds part, the sky breaks into dawn.

The mountains and rivers of the two Zhejiang provinces rest upon the tip of his staff; he has cast off sense-bases and sensory objects in profound stillness. The Great Light hangs in the void, illuminating all that is hidden. Thus it is.
Wandering on pilgrimage; the business of the pilgrimage is finished. Like refined gold tempered a hundred times, it follows the finger’s curve.

The Venerable Zhi-xian: one who possesses wisdom is surely virtuous; the upright does not deviate. This level and even ground of the original nature brightens the sky of my mind. In every turn, movement, bowing, and rising, [it is thus].
The Buddhas appear before you; a single light shines upon all equally, and the myriad phenomena stand forth in their vivid reality.
This is the original face of the Venerable Shanshan—examine it well for yourself. These six kinds of divine functions radiate light day and night; there is no need for deliberation or conjecture.
Be most careful not to take this upon yourself. Before the wind, there is the fragrance of the osmanthus; the golden grain flowers are yellow. Master Xingtan’s refined conduct is gradual and steady;
the Great Way is broad and level. His realization is at the ultimate point of necessity; his application is at the ultimate point of simplicity. From the beginning, [there have been] one thousand...

Seven hundred men, moving freely in all directions—seven forward and eight across. Possessing great capacity and great function, they carry no burden upon their shoulders other than a single horizontal board;
at the crown of their heads, they possess only a single, upright eye. It is like cutting a handful of silk threads: with one cut, they are all cut; everything is completely severed.

The Master Puyi of Yunmen said, "Zhaozhou has no 'two' characters; they have but one meaning. Regarding the eggplant and the *luosu* (cucumber), if you grasp them at once, you will enter directly into the domain of the sages and worthies.
To deliberate upon the sound before it is uttered is still to be caught in the traps of "it is," "it is not," "yes," or "no. Now, listen to the definitive point as I deliver a blow.

Commentary: All are like a superior person who, with effortless ease, extracts a circle of reflections; each is like a pearl rolling upon a jade platter, a brilliant jewel-light shimmering before the wind.
Cold. Who can look from the place of turning? It should respond spontaneously as the occasion arises; do not be deceived by the eyes. The fish’s light shines forth just like anything else;
the moon in the sky bathes in the water below. Brightness and darkness do not interfere with one another.
The Venerable Hōryū said: "The myriad dharmas have no root; from what could they possibly be established? When the single thought-moment is firm, it is like a silver mountain and an iron wall.

One gives rise to the great vow, the banner of great liberation. When ten thousand trees encounter the autumn wind, they naturally grow cool; before the courtyard, a breeze carries the fragrance of osmanthus."
The Venerable Fǎmào’s wild birds and mountain flowers can preach the Dharma; the lush forests and tall bamboos are his disciples. He constantly raised the single word "Mind.
Is it seen face-to-face when the opportunity arises? The clouds bury the night moon; the ice penetrates the jade pitcher. Brightness and darkness are both forgotten.
The identity of principle and phenomena is like trying to catch fish by climbing a tree;
it is utterly futile.
When the Venerable Yunkuan initially gave no promise, Master Kuan set him a strict deadline—like attempting to leap the Yellow River while forcing one's eyes shut, he leaped across.

One cannot leap over it; one must simply carry the wooden board across the shoulders. North and south, the sky is high and the clouds are thin; the autumn colors linger with the fishermen’s songs at evening.
The Master Shangren Sisi first lets go, then takes up the herding. Both nostrils are pierced; all four hooves are shorn. There is a pen, yet no restraint. The mountains themselves—
Blue. The water is naturally green. From the beginning, hunger and satiety have never interfered with one another; within this world of illusions, bubbles, and shadows, cease your frantic toil.
You shall win nothing but this very title.
The Honored One Huixing suddenly attained penetration; his discernment was unimpeded, moving freely in all directions—seven strides forward and eight across.

Having attained great mastery, he turns his entire body within a speck of dust, while his shadow falls beyond the clouds and waters of the Five Lakes. I ask those of the present age: do you understand? A single phrase of clarity.
My son, the Bian jade is without flaw; the pearl from the black dragon is free of blemish.

The Way of Direct Pointing transmitted by the Venerable Master Chuan-yi cannot be conveyed through meaning, for it does not rely on words and letters. It is vividly manifest before one, unobstructed across ten thousand miles.
A single drifting cloud. A vast expanse of bright sun and blue sky. There is meaning before the sound; there is no word after the phrase. Both principle and phenomena are cast aside.
A block of wood, a lump of brick.
Like a person atop a mountain, utterly devoid of even a hair’s breadth of attachment; like a mountain, like a peak; soaring ten thousand miles high, a solitary osprey in the vast void.

Where sight cannot reach—beyond the ends of heaven and the corners of the earth; where intellect cannot fathom—the Great Perfect Enlightenment. The western wind is desolate as yellow leaves fall; ancient...
The hall is deep and silent as the golden bells sway; I regret now that I was deceived at the outset by my travels.

The Chan practitioner Liang of the Shiliang Temple recalls the former Master Liang of the Western Mountain, who once possessed an eloquent exposition on the "Void," yet could not even call back his own head when it turned into a horse.

Master, your model for the monastic community illuminates a thousand ages. You, Venerable One, study Chan and do not study the Teachings; yet from the outset, Chan and the Teachings have no two separate gates.
With a single blow of the fist, you shatter the vast void; those who know the sound need not have it raised again and again.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs praise the appearance of leaving the mountains:
six years of hunger, madness at midnight; a poor child picks up a staff, barefoot and rushing in haste.

Avalokiteśvara soars like a giant turtle upon the ocean currents; the earth is vast and the heavens are clear. With but a single flask of pure water, how can one bring about the complete realization of universal penetration throughout the realms of sentient beings amidst the violent winds of the five turbidities?
The second is to turn back the ear to observe: at night, the sound of waves is transmitted from a distant valley; to turn back the eye to listen: sweet dew is scattered upon the green willows.
Once that which is turned back is forgotten, both observation and listening become tranquil. This is what is called the compassionate power of the vow to save suffering beings.
The Fish Basket Woman walks with light and graceful steps; her hair and makeup are perfectly refined. She manifests great compassion to save sentient beings from suffering.
Her wisdom-eye is pitiable for its total lack of clarity; she merely thinks she is selling glistening scales from within her basket.
The second:
"Clear breeze in the basket; this is one’s livelihood. To seek to exchange fish eyes for bright pearls—who could such a person be? A compassionate Bodhisattva would not do so;
a person of wisdom need not even receive a written notice."
The Maiden of the Horse (A Eulogy for a Person of Jing):
She says in jest that she teaches others to recite the sutras; yet within her breast, the Jing and Wei rivers are clearly distinguished. Countless grains of golden sand cast their reflections;
they scatter as the sound of flowing water at a shallow ford.

Vimalakīrti was emaciated and frail, with a gaunt face and protruding bowels. Suffering from sorrow and affliction, he feigned illness while lying on his bed, preaching the wondrous Dharma of transcending birth and death;
his single silence was peerless.
Dharma’s nine years of wall-gazing revealed the ancestral style; half was sincere, half was empty space. One reed is lost, its whereabouts unknown;
the long river flows east as it has always done.
Buddhabhadra smiles once, and the spring breeze arises. His two eyes are as clear as autumn waters. The sun and moon rest upon the tip of his staff; heaven and earth are contained within his bag.
If Maitreya were suddenly to descend to birth, where would you seek him?

Linji’s eyes were born as triangles; his head was as sharp as the Five Peaks. Three times he suffered the blind staff that broke the donkey’s waist; once he let out a shout into the void, causing the stars and constellations to fall into disarray.
The morning sun pierces the nostrils of the cave; a seamless robe. A single thread of red sunlight—joined together, it is just so. (II)
Tattered and frayed, a broken old relic; one hole patched, then another. As the three-poled red sun pierces through the fence, look at it—how could it weigh less than seven catties?
The Master of the Treasury, rich in self-praised virtues,
requested that [the portrait] be majestic and imposing, brilliant and resplendent— bearing the prophecy of the Lesser Śākyamuni and wearing the imperial robes bestowed [upon him].
Clad in yellow robes, people say that one with virtue may be wealthy; yet he himself was modest regarding his ordinary skills.

With frost and wind upon his two temples, he was as radiant as an elder when invited to dwell at Mupyeong, where he caused the *Haiin* (Ocean Seal) to emit light, as clearly as the sun. He once spoke silently of non-duality before the Sagely Sovereign of the Great Yuan.
The Dharma-gate: silent yet speaking, speaking yet silent. He revived the Daoyang monastic community, a Dharma cave unsurpassed in all under heaven.
Who is it that sees this? It is the Ancient Buddha of Shitou.
Zhitanshi Hall invited Dazhi Dongming.
The Great Way is level and plain; his cast-iron countenance shows no concession to human sentiment. At Yunfeng, the sun shines bright.
